Measuring aid and remittances in small island developing states

From the national figure to the household

Dr Roxane de WaeghMarie Skłodowska-Curie Postdoctoral FellowIslands and Small States InstituteUniversity of Malta
Today, session one

How each kind of money is counted, and where the figures are published

We define aid and remittances, look at what each official figure includes and leaves out, and open every data source on the screen for Tonga. We then ask who decides how each kind of money is used, and how that decision can be seen from the household.

Tomorrow, session two

Your island, mapped

In the first half hour you find three figures for your own country with me in the room. Your group then maps how aid and remittances reach households on your island and presents the map, which is the basis of your classwork and your assignment.

Good afternoon. My name is Roxane de Waegh, and I am a Marie Skłodowska-Curie postdoctoral fellow here at the Islands and Small States Institute. My project, FAR-SIDS, studies foreign aid and remittances in small island developing states, and these two sessions draw on that work.

Today and tomorrow form one piece of work: today I explain how aid and remittances are defined and counted, and I open, on the screen, the websites where the figures for your own country are published. Tomorrow you work in country groups, you find those figures yourselves in the first half hour while I move between the tables, and you then map how the two kinds of money reach households on your island. That map is the material for your classwork and for your assignment, so everything we cover today is something you will use tomorrow. This module uses the terms that economists and ministries use, because you will meet them in every report written about your country. Whenever I use one of those terms for the first time, I will explain it in plain words, and the explanation stays on the screen beside the term.

The question for this week

National figures record how much aid and remittance money reaches an island, but they do not record who received it or who decided how it was spent

Aid, or official development assistanceMoney that a foreign government, or an official body such as the World Bank, gives to your government or lends to it on cheaper terms than a bank would. It is public money that passes between governments.
A remittanceMoney that a relative working abroad sends home to the family. It is private money that passes between people.
A figureA number that an organisation publishes, for example "remittances were 39% of GDP in 2024". Every figure was built by somebody who counted something according to rules.
The national accountsThe government's yearly record of the whole economy: what the country produced, earned and spent, and what came in from other countries and went out to them. The aid and remittance figures are taken from these accounts.

An island receives two kinds of money from outside, the national figures record how much of each arrived, and those figures do not record who received the money or who decided how it was spent. This week we ask what can be known about who received the money and who decided, and today we start with the figures themselves. Aid, which economists call official development assistance, is money that a foreign government or an official body such as the World Bank gives to your government, or lends to it on cheaper terms than a bank would, so it is public money passing between governments. A remittance is money that a relative working abroad sends home, so it is private money passing between people. When your cousin in Auckland sends 200 dollars for school fees, that is a remittance, and when Australia pays for a new road, that is aid.

A figure is a published number, and every figure was built by somebody who counted something according to rules. The national accounts are the government's yearly record of the whole economy, of what the country produced and earned and of what came in from abroad and went out, and the aid and remittance figures quoted in reports are taken from those accounts. In part one we look at how each kind of money is counted and where the figures are published, and I open the real websites for Tonga. In part two we ask why a dollar of aid and a dollar of remittance are used differently, and in part three we move from the national figure to the household and to what a ministry could do with that knowledge.

Part one

How aid and remittances are counted, and where to find the figures for your country

Every published figure follows counting rules. Before you use a figure, you need to know what those rules include, what they leave out, and where the figure for your own country is published.

How each is counted

The four conditions a payment meets to count as aid, and the two kinds of money inside the remittance line.

What each figure leaves out

Donors that report to nobody, and the money and goods that never pass through a bank.

Where your own figures are published

Seven sources, each one opened on the screen for Tonga.

A statement such as "remittances were 39% of GDP" is read as a plain fact about a country, when it is the result of a count, and the rules of that count decide what is included and what is left out. By the end of this part you will be able to find the aid and remittance figures for your own island and explain what each of them measures and what it does not. We start with the scale of the two flows, then define each of them, and then open the websites where your own figures are published.

Part one · The scale of the two flows

Relative to the size of their economies, small island developing states receive more remittances and more aid than other groups of developing countries

The note prints these shares without saying which year they cover or where they came from. The aid shares are for 2020, a pandemic year in which aid increased, and all the shares are averages across a very varied group of countries.

GDP, gross domestic productThe value of everything a country produces in a year, and the usual measure of the size of an economy.
A share of GDPThe figure divided by GDP. Remittances at 8.6% of GDP means that for every 100 dollars the island economy produces in a year, another 8 dollars and 60 cents arrive from relatives abroad.
Sources

United Nations Department of Economic and Social Affairs. (2023). Guidance note: INFFs and Small Island Developing States (SIDS). United Nations. https://sdgs.un.org/sites/default/files/2023-07/INFF%20Guidance_inffs-and-sids.pdf

World Bank. (2020). COVID-19 crisis through a migration lens (Migration and Development Brief No. 32). https://openknowledge.worldbank.org/handle/10986/33634

Ratha, D., Chandra, V., Kim, E. J., Jammeh, K., Riordan, E., & Vezmar, M. (2021). Recovery: COVID-19 crisis through a migration lens (Migration and Development Brief No. 35). World Bank. https://documents1.worldbank.org/curated/en/099738408132414027/pdf/IDU110e1541c1704b14821196441e301ab86ff0b.pdf

GDP, gross domestic product, is the value of everything a country produces inside its own borders in a year, and it is the usual measure of how large an economy is. Remittances are not part of it. That money is earned abroad, by a daughter in Auckland or a son in Sydney, and it arrives on top of what Tonga itself produced. So when a report says remittances are 8.6% of GDP, it means that for every 100 dollars the island economy produced in a year, another 8 dollars and 60 cents came in from relatives working abroad, and the country had 108 dollars and 60 cents to work with rather than 100. The figure is a ratio: money arriving from abroad divided by production at home. A ratio like this can pass 100%, where a share of something never could, and Tonga's has run close to 40%.

One more turn to this matters when you read the figure across several years. The transfer itself never enters GDP, and what the family does with it usually does. Follow the 8 dollars and 60 cents. A mother in Ha'apai spends it on tinned fish at the village shop, on her son's school fees and on a sheet of roofing iron from a hardware store in Nuku'alofa. The shop's trade, the school's teaching and the hardware store's sale are all production inside Tonga, so they are counted in next year's GDP. The money came in once from outside and then circulated inside. That means the two numbers are not independent over time: money from abroad raises production at home, which raises the figure you divide by, so the ratio can fall even when the same amount of money arrives. Within a single year the arithmetic on the screen holds exactly. Across years, read the amount in dollars as well as the ratio.

Across small island developing states that ratio is 8.6%, against 4.6% for the least developed countries, which are the poorest group in the world, and 1.6% for developing countries as a whole. Aid, official development assistance, was 14% of GDP across small island states in 2020, against 13% for the least developed countries (UN DESA, 2023, pp. 8 and 9). All of these are averages across a very varied group of countries, so they describe the scale of the two flows rather than any single island. The note prints the remittance figures without saying which year they cover or where it took them from, and it gives 2020 for the aid figures, a pandemic year in which aid increased. The screen shows both exactly as the note states them.

A figure published under a large name still has to be checked. In April 2020 the World Bank forecast that remittances to low and middle income countries would fall by 19.7% during the pandemic (World Bank, 2020). They fell by 1.7%, and in 2021 they rose by 7.3% (Ratha et al., 2021). Families abroad sent more money, not less, when their relatives at home lost work. Does anyone here know the remittance figure for their own country? Most people do not, and by the middle of this part you will be able to find it in under a minute.

Part one · What counts as aid

A payment counts as aid only if it meets four conditions, and the donor governments set those conditions and report the figures themselves

  1. It comes from a government or an official agency, and not from a charity, a company or a private person.
  2. It goes to a country on the OECD list of aid recipients, which includes every small island developing state except those classed as high income.
  3. Its main purpose is the development and welfare of that country, so military spending and loans that promote the donor's exports do not count.
  4. It is a grant, or a loan on cheaper terms than a bank would give. A grant is money the country keeps and never repays. A loan is repaid, and it is aid only when the interest is lower and the time to repay longer than a bank would offer. A loan at the market interest rate is not aid, even when a government makes it.
OECDThe Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development, an organisation of mostly high income countries based in Paris. Its Development Assistance Committee, the DAC, writes the rules for what counts as aid.
Who counts itEach donor government reports its own spending to the OECD against these rules, so every aid figure for your country is built from what the donors reported.
ConcessionalThe term for a loan on cheaper terms than the market offers, with a lower interest rate and a longer time to repay than a bank would give.
The OECD definition
Sources

OECD. (n.d.). Official development assistance (ODA): Definition and coverage. Retrieved September 17, 2026, from https://www.oecd.org/en/topics/sub-issues/oda-eligibility-and-conditions/official-development-assistance--definition-and-coverage.html

OECD. (2026). Converged statistical reporting directives for the Creditor Reporting System (CRS) and the Annual DAC Questionnaire (DCD/DAC(2026)14/FINAL). https://one.oecd.org/document/DCD/DAC(2026)14/FINAL/en/pdf

The OECD, the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development, is an organisation of mostly high income countries based in Paris, and its Development Assistance Committee, a committee of about thirty donor governments known as the DAC, writes the rules for what counts as aid. Under those rules, a payment is official development assistance only if it meets four conditions.

The payment must come from a government or an official agency rather than from a charity or a company. It must go to a country on the OECD list of aid recipients, and every small island developing state except those classed as high income is on that list. Its main purpose must be the development and welfare of that country, which excludes military spending and loans that promote the donor's exports. Finally, it must be a grant or a cheap loan. A grant is money the country keeps and never repays. A loan is repaid, and it counts as aid only when the interest is lower and the repayment period longer than a bank would offer, which the rules call concessional, so a loan at the market interest rate is not aid even when a government makes it.

The donors also do the counting, since each donor government reports its own spending to the OECD against these rules, so the figure is defined by the governments that send the money, for their own accounting. It names the country that received the money, and it has a box for the agency the money passed through, which can be the recipient government or one of its ministries when the donor fills that box in. Filling it in is optional. Nothing in it reaches a village or a household. So here is a question for you: is a Chinese government loan to Tonga at a commercial interest rate aid? It is not, because it fails the fourth condition, and there is a second reason, which is the subject of the next slide: China does not report to the OECD.

Part one · What the aid figure leaves out

Each row of the OECD figures names the donor that reported it, the country that received the money, the sector it paid for, and two amounts: what was committed and what was disbursed. A donor that does not report to the OECD has no row at all.

The screen shows disbursements, the money actually paid in 2024. The same database also holds the commitment, the amount promised when the agreement was signed, and the two can be years apart.

A donor that does not report

China

China does not report to the OECD, so it has no row. Tonga borrowed from the Export Import Bank of China in 2007 and 2010 and still owed that bank 47% of its external debt in June 2024. That is what Tonga owes, not what China paid in 2024.

Promised money and paid money

Commitments and disbursements

A commitment is the amount promised when an agreement is signed, and a disbursement is the amount actually paid. Payment can arrive years later, or not at all, so ask for disbursements.

Who received it

The country and the sector

A row names the donor, the receiving country, the sector, such as health, roads or education, and the amount. Two further boxes, for the agency the money passed through and for the town or region, are optional and often empty. No row names a village, a household or a person.

Sources

OECD. (2026). Converged statistical reporting directives for the Creditor Reporting System (CRS) and the Annual DAC Questionnaire (DCD/DAC(2026)14/FINAL). https://one.oecd.org/document/DCD/DAC(2026)14/FINAL/en/pdf

World Bank & International Monetary Fund. (2025). Tonga: Joint World Bank–IMF debt sustainability analysis. World Bank. https://documents1.worldbank.org/curated/en/099012326152552028/pdf/BOSIB-caf655fa-adfc-4b75-8ed3-a9712975fdb8.pdf

The OECD database is the most careful record of aid that exists, and it still has gaps that matter for small islands. The largest gap for Tonga is China, which does not report to the OECD. For Tonga the database shows Australia, New Zealand and the World Bank, and the three rows on the screen are the real 2024 disbursements you will pull yourself at slide 13: Australia 68.1 million US dollars, New Zealand 30.6 million and the World Bank's International Development Association 29.6 million. It shows nothing for the Export Import Bank of China. Read the China figure carefully, because it is a different kind of number from the three above it. Australia's 68.1 million is money paid in one year. The China figure is a debt: 47% of everything Tonga still owed abroad in June 2024 (World Bank and IMF, 2025). External debt is the money a country owes to lenders in other countries, and Tonga's total was about 157 million US dollars, so roughly 74 million of it is owed to that one bank. It comes from two loans, one signed in 2007 to rebuild the Nuku'alofa business district after the riots of 2006 and one signed in 2010 for the national road improvement, both at 2% interest with about five years before repayments began and twenty years to repay. Those terms are cheaper than a bank's, so the loans would meet the fourth condition we set out on the last slide, and they are absent from the table only because China does not report. Tonga has taken on no new external loans since 2011, which is how one lender can hold almost half the debt while paying out nothing recent. The Lowy Institute, which does not wait for donors to report, counts China as 18% of everything Tonga received between 2008 and 2024, and I will open that map later in this part.

The database also separates commitments from disbursements, where a commitment is the amount promised on the day an agreement is signed and a disbursement is the amount actually paid out. The two can be years apart, so when you take a figure from the database, you should ask for disbursements. Finally, every row of the database names the donor, the country that received the money, the sector, such as health, roads or education, and the amount. The reporting rules also give donors one optional box of 100 characters, called the geographical target area, for the town or region a project is meant to benefit, and donors rarely fill it (OECD, 2026). Nothing in the database names a village, a household or a person. This is also one of the reasons we are looking at aid and remittances at the household level, because so few studies have done it.

Part one · What counts as a remittance

Central banks count remittances by adding up what the banks and money transfer companies say they received from abroad

What the remittance line adds together
Part one · Personal transfers

Money sent by someone who has lived abroad for a year or more.

For example, a cousin in Auckland for ten years.
+
Part two · Compensation of employees

The pay of someone working abroad on a contract of less than a year.

For example, a seasonal worker picking fruit.

Together, the two parts make up the remittance line of the balance of payments.

The companies whose reports build the figure
The balance of paymentsThe record that every central bank keeps of the money that crosses the border in a year, in both directions: exports, imports, loans, aid and remittances. GDP counts what is produced inside the country; the balance of payments counts what moves in and out of it. Remittances are one line of this record, made of the two parts above.
The one year ruleA person abroad for a year or more counts as living in the other country, so what they send home is a transfer. A person abroad for less than a year still counts as living at home, so their whole pay is counted as income, whether or not they send it home.
How the figure is builtBanks and money transfer companies report to the central bank the money they received from abroad and handed over here, and the central bank adds those reports together. No household is asked what it received.
TongaThe National Reserve Bank of Tonga publishes remittances in four categories, and the pay of Tongans working abroad, which is where the seasonal workers appear, is one of them.
Sources

Bank of Jamaica. (n.d.). List of remittance companies. Retrieved September 18, 2026, from https://boj.org.jm/core-functions/financial-system/list-of-remittance-companies/

da Cruz, V., Fengler, W., & Schwartzman, A. (2004). Remittances to Comoros: Volume, trends, impact and implications (Africa Region Working Paper Series No. 75). World Bank. https://documents1.worldbank.org/curated/en/957391468772177750/pdf/312750PAPER0Comoros0AFR0wp75.pdf

International Monetary Fund. (n.d.). Annex 4: Remittances [Draft annex to the balance of payments and international investment position manual, 7th ed.]. Retrieved September 17, 2026, from https://www.imf.org/-/media/files/data/statistics/bmp7/draft-chapters/bpm7-annex-4-v7-remittances.pdf

National Reserve Bank of Tonga. (n.d.). Economic reviews: monthly economic update and remittances. Retrieved September 18, 2026, from https://www.reservebank.to/

Remittances are counted in a different way, through the balance of payments that every central bank keeps, which is the record of all the money that came into the country and went out of it during a year, including exports, imports, loans, aid and remittances. GDP, which we met two slides ago, counts what is produced inside the country. The balance of payments counts what crosses the border, so remittances appear in the second and never in the first. Remittances are one line of that record, and the line adds two parts together. The first is personal transfers, which is the money sent home by someone who has lived abroad for a year or more, such as a cousin who has been in Auckland for ten years. The second is what accountants call compensation of employees, which is the pay of someone working abroad on a contract of less than a year, such as a Tongan woman on a seven month contract picking fruit in Australia. Her whole pay is counted, whether or not she sends it home, because under the one year rule she still counts as living in Tonga (IMF, n.d., Annex 4).

The figure is built from reports. The banks and the money transfer companies on the screen, the ones your families actually use, tell the central bank how much money they received from abroad and handed over here, and the central bank adds those reports together. MoneyGram and Western Union carry most of the money sent to Tonga and to Jamaica: a survey of Pacific workers put MoneyGram at 54% and Western Union at 20% of transfers on the Australia to Tonga corridor. Remitly and Ria are among the companies priced on the France to Comoros corridor, where Western Union has long been the largest. No household is asked what it received. So the method misses any transfer that does not pass through one of these companies, which is the next slide. The National Reserve Bank of Tonga publishes remittances in four categories, and the pay of Tongans working abroad, seasonal workers among them, is one of them, so you can see that pay separately from money a cousin sends. Watch for that kind of change when you read a series over time: when a central bank starts recording a category separately, or starts capturing something it used to miss, the published total can move without anything changing in the households.

Part one · What the remittance figure leaves out

The remittance figure leaves out money and goods that never pass through a bank or a money transfer company

Cash carried by hand

Cash in a suitcase

Money brought home on a visit, or given to a friend who is travelling, never passes through a bank or a transfer company, so nobody reports it.

Goods sent instead of money

The barrel

A barrel of food, a laptop or a pair of school shoes is a real transfer, and no line of the balance of payments records it.

Bills paid from abroad

The school fee

When a relative pays a school fee or a hospital bill directly from abroad, the household never handles the money, so nobody reports it.

A question for you

Who has sent or received something from a relative abroad that was not money in a bank? What was it, and who decided what to send?

Sources

Das, A., Brown, L., McFarlane, A., & Campbell, K. (2021). Remittances and reverse flows in Jamaica. The Journal of Developing Areas, 55(4), 211–233. https://doi.org/10.1353/jda.2021.0087

Before I give you the list, give me your own examples, in the word you use at home. If you are from Jamaica you know the barrel that comes by ship. If you are from Tonga or Samoa you know the box or the parcel that comes back with a relative, and the money collected for a funeral or a church donation. If you are from the Comoros you know cash carried by hand between Marseille and Moroni. Cash carried by hand, in a suitcase on a visit home or given to a friend who is travelling, never passes through a bank. Goods sent instead of money, such as a barrel of food, a laptop or school shoes, are real transfers that no line in the balance of payments records. Bills paid directly from abroad, such as a school fee or a hospital bill settled from Auckland or Miami, never reach the household as money, so the household never reports them.

Thus the official figure is the smallest amount that households could have received, and the true amount is larger by an amount that nobody knows. The figure also counts the money coming in without subtracting what goes out again. Das and colleagues followed the extra dollar after it reaches Jamaica and found that about 24 cents of it leaves the country again (Das et al., 2021). It leaves in three ways: the government and firms use foreign currency to pay what they owe to lenders abroad, the central bank holds some of it as reserves rather than letting it circulate at home, and some is moved out by people who are able to move money. None of that is the transfer company's fee, which is taken before the money ever reaches the household, and the fee is the next slide.

Part one · What the transfer costs

Families pay to send money home, and on the Tonga corridors that cost is around 8 dollars in every 100

The cost is the company’s fee plus the margin it takes on the exchange rate. The bars are averages across the providers surveyed in each corridor.

The target

Under 3% by 2030

Sustainable Development Goal 10 commits governments to bring the cost below 3% and to end corridors above 5%. The world average was 6.36% in the third quarter of 2025.

The same corridor

1.62% or 12.58%

From New Zealand to Tonga the cheapest operator charged 1.62% and a bank charged 12.58%. From Australia the cheapest charged 0.92% and one bank 22.49%. The average hides that choice.

What the target is worth

A$79 million a year

The Lowy Institute estimates that households in Fiji, Tonga and Vanuatu together would keep about this much more each year if their corridors met the 3% target.

Discuss

Should it cost anything to send your own wages home to your family, and if the transfer is digital, why does the price stay this high?

Sources

Every figure we have used so far is the money that arrived. Some of what the family sent never arrives, because the company that carries it keeps a part.

Sending 200 US dollars from New Zealand to Tonga cost 7.89% in the third quarter of 2025, and 7.65% from Australia. From the United States to Jamaica it cost 6.06%, and from France to the Comoros 3.78%. The world average was 6.36%. The cost is made of two things: the fee the company charges, and the exchange rate it gives you, which is usually a little worse than the rate on the screen at the bank, and that difference is part of what you pay.

Governments agreed a target on this. Sustainable Development Goal 10 commits countries to bring the cost of sending money home below 3% by 2030, and to end corridors that cost more than 5%. The world is at roughly double the target, and the United Nations reported in 2025 that it had risen rather than fallen the year before.

Two things here are worth arguing about. First, the average hides a wide spread. In the same New Zealand to Tonga corridor the cheapest operator charged 1.62% and a bank charged 12.58%, and from Australia the cheapest charged 0.92% and one bank 22.49%, so what a family pays depends on which counter it walks up to and whether it can use a phone. Devpolicy researchers argue from this that the simple average overstates what a careful sender actually pays. Second, the reasons the cost stays high are structural rather than greedy: banks have closed the accounts of small transfer companies to avoid the compliance risk of money laundering rules, the volumes in island corridors are small, most transfers still start or end in cash, and in several markets one or two companies hold most of the business.

So the question on the screen is for you. The Lowy Institute estimates that households in Fiji, Tonga and Vanuatu would keep about 79 million Australian dollars a year more if the 3% target were met, which is larger than some of the aid programmes we will look at this afternoon. Who should carry that cost: the companies, the banks, the sending governments or the families? And as you argue, notice who in that list has the least room to refuse.

Part one · What the transfer costs · Demonstration 1 of 9

Remittance Prices Worldwide lists what every company charges to carry money from one country to another

How much of the money a family sends home does the transfer company keep, and does the price depend on which company the family uses?

The New Zealand to Tonga corridor on remittanceprices.worldbank.org
Remittance Prices Worldwide, New Zealand to TongaUnited States to JamaicaFrance to the Comoros
The clicks, in order
  1. Open remittanceprices.worldbank.org. At the top of the page choose the country the money is sent from and the country it is sent to, and click Go. The site calls each pair of countries a corridor: New Zealand to Tonga is one corridor, United States to Jamaica is another.
  2. Above the table click USD, then the tab 200.00 USD. Every company is then priced for the same transfer of 200 US dollars, so any two corridors can be compared.
  3. Read the column Total cost (%). It adds the fee the company charges to the exchange rate margin, which is the difference between the exchange rate the company gives and the rate at which the two currencies are actually traded. The site prints the fee in dollars and the margin as a percentage, so compare companies on the Total cost column only.
  4. Find the lowest and the highest numbers in the Total cost (%) column and read the company name at the start of each row. The last column, Total cost (USD), gives the same cost in dollars.
  5. Read the line to the right of the heading. It says in which week the prices were collected, so the table is a snapshot of one week, not an average of the year.

The target is under 3% by 2030. The Sustainable Development Goals set it. The France to Comoros corridor already meets it and the New Zealand to Tonga corridor charges more than twice it, so the poorest corridor is not automatically the most expensive.

What this source cannot tell you. What any particular family actually paid, or whether it used a company on the list at all. Cash carried home by hand appears in none of these tables.

Why this matters

On the New Zealand to Tonga corridor, a family sending 200 US dollars a month pays the cheapest company on the list 5.54 dollars a month in transfer costs, about 66 dollars a year, and pays the most expensive company 35.26 dollars a month, about 423 dollars a year, for exactly the same transfer. The difference, about 357 dollars a year, depends only on which company the sender chooses. If your family sends or receives money, this table shows what the company they use charges beside every other company on the same corridor.

Sources

World Bank. (2025). Remittance Prices Worldwide, third quarter 2025. Retrieved September 18, 2026, from https://remittanceprices.worldbank.org/

Every figure so far is money that arrived. This site shows what the transfer company took out before it arrived. I am opening remittanceprices.worldbank.org now; open it with me. At the top of the page, choose the country the money is sent from and the country it is sent to, and click Go. The site calls each pair of countries a corridor, so New Zealand to Tonga is one corridor and France to the Comoros is another. I am choosing New Zealand and Tonga.

Above the table, click USD and then 200.00 USD, so that every company is priced for the same transfer of 200 US dollars. Now read the Kiwibank row with me, because the columns catch people out. The Fee column is in dollars: 26.92 dollars on a 200 dollar transfer, which is 13.46%. The Exchange rate margin column is already a percentage, 4.17%. The margin is the difference between the exchange rate the company gives you and the rate at which the two currencies are actually traded, and no company prints it on the receipt. Add the two and you have the Total cost column, 17.63%, and the last column turns that back into money: 35.26 dollars out of the 200. The Total cost column is the only one to compare.

Now look at the spread rather than the average. On this corridor the cheapest company charges 2.77% and the most expensive, a bank at the branch counter, charges 17.63% for the identical transfer. A family sending 200 dollars a month pays the cheapest company 5.54 dollars a month in transfer costs, about 66 dollars a year, and pays the most expensive company 35.26 dollars a month, about 423 dollars a year. The difference is about 357 dollars a year, a term of school fees in Tonga, and it depends only on which counter the sender walks up to. If your family sends or receives money, which company do they use, and has anyone in the family ever compared? Take a moment on that.

One more thing on this site may surprise you. The France to the Comoros corridor, to the poorest of our three countries, is cheaper than the New Zealand to Tonga corridor, and it already meets the 2030 target of under 3%. The cost of a transfer follows how many companies compete on a route and how many customers use it, not how poor the receiving country is.

If this page has moved by the time you look for it, search Remittance Prices Worldwide and use the Corridors menu at the top of the site. If your island is not one of our three, the site covers only the corridors with the largest flows, so yours may be missing. If it is, say so in your map, then look for the nearest comparable corridor from the same sending country and label it as a substitute. Never quote a corridor you did not check as though it were yours.

Part one · How the survey question changes the figure

How many households a survey finds receiving remittances depends on what the survey asked them

Each bar is the share of Tongan households that had received money from abroad in the year before they were asked. The 2001 and 2021 counts come from Tonga’s national household surveys, which asked about cash only. The 2004 count comes from Brown and Leeves, who surveyed 500 Tongan households and asked about goods, school fees and bills paid for the household as well as cash.

What the three counts showIn 2001 the national survey asked one question about cash, and 75 in every hundred Tongan households said they had received money from abroad in the previous year. In 2004 Brown and Leeves asked many questions, covering money, goods, school fees and bills paid for the household, and 90 in every hundred had received something. In 2021 the national survey asked the single cash question again and also found 90 in every hundred, so more households really were receiving money than in 2001.
Who receives, 2021Of every hundred Tongan households headed by a woman, 96 received cash from relatives abroad in the previous twelve months. Of every hundred headed by a man, 88 did. A third of that money was sent from New Zealand and a third from Australia.
Households with nobody abroad, 200433 in every hundred Tongan households had no family member living abroad and still received money from relatives overseas, because money travels along family networks beyond the house the migrant left.
Sources

Brown, R. P. C., & Leeves, G. (2011). Comparative effects of migrants’ remittances on composition of recipient household income in two small, island economies. Applied Economics, 43(27), 3965–3976. https://doi.org/10.1080/00036841003742611

Tonga Statistics Department. (2022). Tonga 2021 household income and expenditure survey report. https://tongastats.gov.to/download/47/household-income-expenditure-survey/8078/tonga-2021-hies-report.pdf

In a household survey, a statistics office visits a sample of households, asks the same questions in every house, and publishes the answers as figures for the whole country. It is the only source that counts households rather than dollars, and what it finds depends on the wording of the question.

Tonga has three of these counts. The national survey of 2001 asked one general question about cash sent from abroad, and 75 in every hundred households said yes. Three years later two economists, Richard Brown and Gareth Leeves, surveyed 500 Tongan households about what they had received during 2004, and they asked many questions instead of one: money sent, goods sent, school fees paid for the household, bills settled from abroad, and transfers that people do not think of as remittances at all. Ninety in every hundred households had received something (Brown and Leeves, 2011, Table 2 on p. 3968). The two surveys are three years apart and fifteen households in a hundred apart, and the authors put almost all of that gap down to the questions rather than to any change in Tongan families.

Then the national survey of 2021 asked the narrow question again, about cash received in the last twelve months, and this time 90 in every hundred households said yes (Tonga Statistics Department, 2022, pp. 21 and 22, Figure 37). The narrow question in 2021 found what only the detailed questionnaire had found in 2004, so between 2001 and 2021 the number of households receiving money from abroad really did rise, and receiving has become close to universal.

The 2021 survey also reports who receives. Of every hundred households headed by a woman, 96 received cash, against 88 of every hundred headed by a man, and a third of the money came from New Zealand and a third from Australia. The 2004 survey adds one more finding that matters for tomorrow: 33 in every hundred households had nobody living abroad and still received money, because it travels along family networks beyond the house the migrant left. More households receive than have a migrant of their own.

So before you compare two years, or two countries, find the question each survey asked. Two numbers that look like the same measure are often answers to different questions.

Part one · The rule for every figure

Beside every figure you use, write what it measures, the year, and where you found it

Gross and netGross aid is what arrived. Net aid subtracts what the country repaid that year on earlier aid loans. The OECD database reports gross aid and the World Bank series reports net aid, so the two figures follow different rules.
GDP and GNIAid shares are usually divided by GNI, gross national income, which is GDP plus what residents earn abroad minus what foreigners earn inside the country. Remittance shares are usually divided by GDP. Say which one you used.
One year and several yearsTonga's net aid was half of national income in 2022, the year of the Hunga Tonga eruption, and a fifth in 2023. A single year shows one point, and only several years show whether that year is part of a pattern.
The ruleWrite the rule, the year and the source in the same sentence as the figure, in your classwork and in your assignment.
Sources

OECD. (n.d.). CRS: Creditor Reporting System (flows) [Data set]. OECD Data Explorer. Retrieved September 18, 2026, from https://data-explorer.oecd.org/

World Bank. (n.d.). Net ODA received (% of GNI) (DT.ODA.ODAT.GN.ZS) [Data set]. World Development Indicators. Retrieved September 17, 2026, from https://data.worldbank.org/indicator/DT.ODA.ODAT.GN.ZS?locations=TO

World Bank. (n.d.). Net official development assistance received (current US$) (DT.ODA.ODAT.CD) [Data set]. World Development Indicators. Retrieved September 17, 2026, from https://data.worldbank.org/indicator/DT.ODA.ODAT.CD?locations=TO

Every figure in your classwork and your assignment has to follow one rule: beside it, you write what it measures, the year, and where you found it. The Tongan figures on the screen show what goes wrong without the rule, and they are the figures students most often confuse. Gross aid counts what arrived, which was 150.9 million US dollars for Tonga in 2024 in the OECD database, while net aid subtracts what Tonga repaid that year on earlier aid loans, which was 129.5 million in 2023 in the World Bank series. The two figures differ by rule and by year, so they cannot stand side by side without saying which is which, and students confuse them more often than any other pair because the two largest databases use different rules by default.

Aid shares are usually divided by GNI, gross national income, which starts from GDP, adds the income residents earn abroad, and subtracts the income foreigners earn inside the country, whereas remittance shares are usually divided by GDP. In an economy that depends on remittances the two totals can differ, so the share changes with the choice, and you need to say which one you used. A figure also needs its year. Tonga's net aid was 50.7% of national income in 2022 and 20.3% in 2023, and both are right. In January 2022 the Hunga Tonga volcano erupted and sent a tsunami across Tongatapu, and donors paid for the repairs, so the total for that year was far above anything usual. One year tells you where a country stood at one moment. Several years tell you whether that moment was ordinary.

Three islands, three positions. Tonga receives a fifth of its national income in aid, the Comoros a ninth, and Jamaica almost none.

What this source cannot tell you. Who paid it. This page gives one total for all donors together, and the next demonstration breaks that total into the donors that paid it.

Why this matters

This is the figure every report quotes when it says how dependent an island is on aid, and it is one line on one page. Tonga at 20.3% of national income, the Comoros at 11.3% and Jamaica at 0.4% in 2023 tell you at once that aid is not shared out by need. The grey text under the title tells you that the OECD counted the money and the World Bank divided it by the size of the economy, so this demonstration and the next one are the same count read in two places.

Sources

World Bank. (n.d.). Net ODA received (% of GNI) [Data set]. World Bank Open Data. Retrieved September 18, 2026, from https://data.worldbank.org/indicator/DT.ODA.ODAT.GN.ZS

I am opening the link on this slide, which lands on the World Bank page for Tonga, and I would like you to open it on your own laptop as we go. This page gives one number for each country for each year: all the aid the country received that year, after subtracting what it repaid on earlier aid loans, divided by its national income. National income, which the page calls GNI, is everything the country produced plus what its people earned abroad, minus what foreigners earned inside it. Dividing by it is what lets a small island be compared with a large country.

Follow the five clicks on the slide with me. When you type in the search box, a list drops down as you type, and the line you want reads exactly Net ODA received (% of GNI). One line away from it sits Net ODA provided, which is what donor countries give away, and if you click that one by mistake you get an empty map, because Tonga gives no aid. The page opens for the whole world, so scroll down to the list called All Countries and Economies and click your country, and the chart redraws for it. I am doing that now for Tonga, and now for Jamaica, so you can see the whole page change. That is how you switch country.

Now read the grey text under the title with me. It says the numbers come from the Development Assistance Committee of the OECD, and that World Bank estimates of national income are used for the bottom of the division. So this page and the OECD page in the next demonstration are not two organisations counting separately. They are the same donor returns, with the World Bank dividing them by its own estimate of the size of the economy. When the two disagree it is because one is gross and the other is net, or because one was revised later, and never because two counts of the same money came out differently.

Look at the gap between the three islands on the slide: Tonga at 20.3, the Comoros at 11.3 and Jamaica at 0.4 in 2023. Why does an island in the Caribbean receive so little aid compared with an island in the Pacific of similar size? Think about that for a moment before I say anything. The answer that matters for this module is that aid is not allocated by need alone.

If this page has moved by the time you look for it, search for the exact phrase Net ODA received % of GNI World Bank, and the first result is this page. If your island is not one of our three, it is on this same page, because every country in the world is in the list under the chart.

Sources

OECD. (n.d.). CRS: Creditor Reporting System (flows) [Data set]. OECD Data Explorer. Retrieved September 18, 2026, from https://data-explorer.oecd.org/

The link on this slide lands on the finished table for Tonga. I am going to clear the filters and build it again from the beginning, so you can see where each number comes from, and you can build it with me.

First, what this database is. It holds one row for every project that a reporting donor funded, anywhere in the world, going back decades. The filters on the left decide which rows you see, and three of them decide everything: who received the money, who gave it, and in which year.

The donor step is the one that goes wrong. The database opens with the donors collapsed into one line called DAC countries, which gives one number and hides the list. Deselect All followed by Select All is what opens the list out. The site only offers donors that actually paid this country, so Select All is safe here and will not give you the whole world.

Look at the shape of the table, because it is a tree rather than a flat list. Official donors is everything. Underneath it sit DAC countries, then Non-DAC countries, then Multilateral organisations, and under each of those the individual donors. Australia is already inside DAC countries, and the International Development Association is already inside Multilateral organisations, so if you add the individual rows to the group rows you count the same money twice.

Now the words at the top of the table, which you should write down: gross disbursements, constant 2024 prices. Gross means before subtracting anything the country repaid, so this figure is larger than the World Bank net figure in the previous demonstration for the same country and the same year. Constant prices means the amounts have been adjusted so that years can be compared. Disbursements means money actually paid, as against commitments, which is money promised and may arrive years later or not at all.

When you click Download, you get a file with one row for every line of this table and a lot of empty columns. Ignore the empty ones. The three things you need are the donor name, the year and the amount, and the amount is in millions of US dollars, so 68.068 on the Australia row is 68 million dollars.

Now, in your group, find the three largest donors to your own island. Is any of them a country you would not have guessed?

If this page has moved by the time you look for it, search for OECD Data Explorer CRS Creditor Reporting System, and the dataset is reached through Topic, then Development, then Official Development Assistance, then the first entry in the list. If your island is not one of our three, it is in the Recipient filter, and the four entries you see when you search for it are the same four groupings for every island: tick the first one.

  2. China reports to nobody. Open china.aiddata.org.

  4. Read the two figures at the top of the page: Projects/Activities, the number of projects, and Commitments (USD, cumulative), the money China promised. The grey note in the left panel gives the basis: constant 2023 US dollars, all years since 2000 added together.

Tonga

In the OECD table, the Comoros receives 17.685 million from non-DAC governments in 2024, of which Saudi Arabia 11.281 and the United Arab Emirates 6.188.

Do not add these to the OECD figure. The OECD figure is money paid in one year at 2024 prices. AidData is money promised since 2000 at 2023 prices. Two different questions, two different answers.

What this source cannot tell you. How much of the promised money has actually been paid out, and which household any of it reached. Every source on this slide counts money at the level of the country or the project.

Why this matters

None of China’s 419 million dollars to Tonga appears in the OECD table or in the World Bank aid share, so a student who uses only those two sources leaves out the largest single lender to the country. In the downloaded file, 142 of Tonga’s 180 Chinese projects are grants and only 5 are loans, but the two largest loans, 96 million dollars for the Nuku’alofa business district in 2007 and 55 million for roads in 2010, are worth more than all 142 grants together. The list reads like a list of gifts, and most of the money is debt.

Sources

AidData. (n.d.). Global Chinese Development Finance Dashboard. William & Mary. Retrieved September 18, 2026, from https://china.aiddata.org/

OECD. (n.d.). CRS: Creditor Reporting System (flows) [Data set]. OECD Data Explorer. Retrieved September 18, 2026, from https://data-explorer.oecd.org/

This slide exists because the OECD figures are built from what donors report, and reporting is voluntary. A government that does not report has no row, and its money is missing from every figure built on that database, including the World Bank aid share in the aid share demonstration. China is the largest such donor, and it does not report.

Start with the part of the OECD table that most people scroll past, the branch called Non-DAC countries. These governments report even though they are not members of the committee. Open the table for the Comoros and you find Saudi Arabia at 11.3 million and the United Arab Emirates at 6.2 million sitting there, so those governments are not missing, they are under a heading nobody opens.

For China we need a different site. Open china.aiddata.org with me. Click Filters & Search, then Geographic Filters, then the tab Countries; type Tonga, tick it, and click Update Filters. Two figures appear at the top: 180 projects, and 419 million US dollars committed. Now I am doing the same for Jamaica: 129 projects and 2.4 billion dollars. Two and a half billion dollars of Chinese commitments to Jamaica appear nowhere in the aid figures you would otherwise find for Jamaica. That is the point of this slide.

Be careful with the word commitment. AidData counts commitments and the OECD table counted disbursements. A commitment is money promised in an agreement; a disbursement is money paid. Tonga’s 419 million is what China promised over twenty five years, not what arrived last year, and putting it beside the OECD’s 150.9 million for 2024 compares two different things. If you use both figures, label both.

Now click Download Data and open the file named CLG_Global1.0_Filtered. It has one row per Chinese project in Tonga since 2000, 180 rows, and far more columns than anyone needs. Look only at three: Title, Flow_Type and Amount_Constant_USD_2023. Click the heading of the Flow_Type column and sort it A to Z, so that the loans sit together: 142 of the 180 rows say Grant and only 5 say Loan. So is China generous to Tonga? Most people say yes at this point. Now sort by Amount_Constant_USD_2023, largest first, and read the top two rows: a 96 million dollar loan from China Eximbank in 2007 for the Nuku’alofa central business district, and a 55 million dollar loan in 2010 for roads. Those two loans are worth more than all 142 grants together. The grants are school buildings, sports fields, scholarships and disaster supplies, real things, and almost all of them small; the money is in the loans, and loans are repaid. Tonga’s whole economy is about 650 million dollars a year.

Here is the question to sit with. A government that looks at this list sees 142 gifts and 5 loans. The same government, ten years later, is repaying the loans out of a budget that also has to pay for schools and clinics. Who in the country is carrying those two loans today, and did the households that received the gifts have any say in the loans that came with them? There is no single right answer, and you will meet the repayment figure again on the Tonga slide this afternoon.

If a page has moved by the time you look, search AidData China global development finance dashboard. If your island is not one of our three, the pair of sources is the same everywhere: the Non-DAC branch of the OECD table for governments that report, and AidData for China. If your island has a large lender that appears in neither, say so in your map and name where you looked, because that absence is itself a finding.

The central bank’s own figure for Tonga, from the spreadsheet in step 1, sheet New Remittances, row 2024, column Total: 524.8 million pa’anga, which is about 221 million US dollars at the 2024 exchange rate of 2.37. The World Bank line for the same year reads 253.8 million US dollars, 39.2% of GDP. The two do not match; both go in the notes with the source and the year.

Set these beside the aid figures from the aid share demonstration. Tonga receives 39.2% of GDP in remittances against 20.3% of national income in aid. Jamaica receives 16.2% against 0.4%. In all three countries the families send more than the donors give, and in Jamaica they send forty times more.

What this source cannot tell you. Which households received it, or how many of them there are. The whole line is a total for the country, built from what companies reported, and the household survey demonstration is the only source that counts households.

Why this matters

The World Bank share is the figure every report quotes, and it is built from what the central bank counted, divided by the World Bank’s own estimate of the size of the economy. For Tonga in 2024 the central bank’s own figure gives 34% of GDP and the World Bank’s gives 39%. Both are right for what each one counts. A ministry that quotes one without the other cannot explain the gap; a student who writes both down, with the source and the year beside each, can.

Sources

World Bank. (n.d.). Personal remittances, received (% of GDP) [Data set]. World Bank Open Data. Retrieved September 18, 2026, from https://data.worldbank.org/indicator/BX.TRF.PWKR.DT.GD.ZS

National Reserve Bank of Tonga. (n.d.). Remittances [Data set]. Retrieved September 18, 2026, from https://www.reservebank.to/

Bank of Jamaica. (n.d.). Remittances [Data set]. Retrieved September 18, 2026, from https://boj.org.jm/statistics/external-sector/remittances/

Banque Centrale des Comores. (2023, January 19). Statistiques de la balance des paiements. Retrieved September 18, 2026, from https://banque-comores.km/page/show/statistiques-de-la-balance-des-paiements

We go to the central bank first, and there is a reason for the order. The central bank is the body that actually counts the money: the banks and money transfer companies in the country report to it what they received from abroad, and it adds those reports together. The World Bank does not repeat that count. It takes the figure through the IMF balance of payments returns, adds its own estimate where a country has not reported, and divides by its own estimate of GDP. The grey line on the World Bank page says exactly that.

I am opening the Tonga central bank now, reservebank.to, and under Economic Reviews you can see Remittances sitting in the menu. Clicking it downloads the bank's own spreadsheet. Open it with me, because this is the step people find hardest, and every central bank file has the same three traps.

First trap, the sheet. This file has three tabs. The one to use is New Remittances, because the note at the foot of it says it follows the current IMF definition, and the tab called Old Remittances stops in 2014. Second trap, the row. The yearly totals sit in the block at the top, one row per year, and the monthly figures below them are only there if you want a month. Find the row 2024. Third trap, the column and the unit. The column called Total gives 524.8, and the line under the title says the unit: million, in the currency of the country, so this is 524.8 million pa’anga, not dollars. There is a fourth trap on this particular sheet. The middle block, Remittances by currency, has a column called USD, and it is not the total in US dollars. It is the part of the money that arrived as US dollars, still written in pa’anga, beside the parts that arrived as Australian and New Zealand dollars, and the four columns add up to the Total. So write down 524.8 million pa’anga as the central bank's figure.

Now put it beside the World Bank line, which is in US dollars. Divide by the year's average exchange rate, 2.37 pa’anga to the dollar in 2024, which the World Bank publishes as Official exchange rate on the same site, and 524.8 million becomes about 221 million US dollars. The World Bank line says 253.8 million US dollars for the same year, about 15% more, and that is why the World Bank share is 39.2% of GDP while the central bank's figure gives 34%. We cannot tell from these two pages why they differ. The World Bank takes its figure from the IMF balance of payments, and the IMF may include money the central bank does not see in its reports from banks and transfer companies. Both numbers are correct for what each one counts, so you write both down, with the source and the year, and a gap between them is a question for the ministry, not an error to hide.

The rule for any island is short. Find the sheet that follows the current definition, the row for the year, the column called Total or Personal transfers, and the unit line at the top that says the currency and whether the figures are in millions. Every central bank file has those four things, however it is laid out.

The three central banks are three levels of detail, and that is the real lesson of this slide. Tonga publishes a spreadsheet running from 1993 that separates seasonal workers’ earnings from money a relative sends. Jamaica publishes remittances by parish, which is the only sub-national remittance figure any of these three countries has. The Comoros publishes a balance of payments spreadsheet that ends in 2021 and is built on the fifth edition of the IMF manual rather than the sixth. All three are doing the same job with different resources.

Look at the aid and remittance shares side by side on the slide. In every one of these islands the families send home more than the donors give, and no ministry has a department for it.

If a page has moved by the time you look, search for your country’s name and the words central bank remittances, and look for the bank’s own address rather than a news article. For the World Bank series search Personal remittances received % of GDP World Bank. If your island is not one of our three, its central bank still publishes a balance of payments, because the IMF requires it. Look for a menu called Statistics, Economic Reviews, Publications or Research. The remittance line may be called personal transfers, workers’ remittances, secondary income or, in French, transferts courants. If the bank publishes only a quarterly report as a PDF, which is common, search that PDF for the word remittance or transfert and take the figure from the table, writing down which quarter it covers.

Part one · Where to find the figures · Demonstration 7 of 9

The United Nations counts how many people born in your country live abroad, and the World Bank counts how many live at home

How many people from your island are abroad to send the money, and how many of them are women and men?

The International Migrant Stock page of the United Nations Population Division, with the Total, origin file under Data
UN DESA, International Migrant StockWorld Bank, Population, total, Tonga
The clicks, in order
  1. Open un.org/development/desa/pd, choose Data in the top menu, then International Migrant Stock.
  2. Under Data on the right of the page, click Total, origin. A spreadsheet downloads. Open the sheet called Table 1.
  3. Find your country’s row. The years 1990 to 2024 run three times across the row: both sexes first, then men, then women, so the row has three columns headed 2024. You want all three: the total, the men and the women.
  4. For the number of people living at home, open data.worldbank.org, type Population, total in the search box, click the line with that name, and click your country in the list under the chart.
  5. Write the four numbers down with their year: people abroad, men abroad, women abroad, and people at home.
What you should see

People born in Tonga living abroad in 2024, from the United Nations, and people living in Tonga in 2024, from the World Bank.

Tonga, abroad

Jamaica: 550,194 men and 698,318 women abroad, against 2,839,175 people at home. The Comoros: 169,412 men and 198,162 women abroad, against 866,628 at home.

What this source cannot tell you. Who sends money and who does not. The file counts people who live abroad, not people who send, and a person abroad who sends nothing is counted the same as one who sends every month.

Why this matters

For every 100 people living in Tonga, 51 people born in Tonga live abroad. For Jamaica the figure is 44 for every 100 at home, and for the Comoros 42. The remittance figure on the last slide is sent by these people, so a ministry that knows how many are abroad, and how many of them are women and men, knows the size of the group behind the money. Men are the majority abroad from Tonga and women the majority from Jamaica and the Comoros, and the difference matters because who is abroad decides who is missing from the household at home.

Sources

United Nations, Department of Economic and Social Affairs, Population Division. (2024). International Migrant Stock 2024. Retrieved September 20, 2026, from https://www.un.org/development/desa/pd/content/international-migrant-stock

World Bank. (n.d.). Population, total (SP.POP.TOTL) [Data set]. World Development Indicators. Retrieved September 20, 2026, from https://data.worldbank.org/indicator/SP.POP.TOTL?locations=TO

The last slide gave you the money that families send home. This slide gives you the people who send it, and it takes two minutes once you know where the numbers are. I am opening un.org/development/desa/pd; choose Data in the top menu, then International Migrant Stock. On the right of the page, under Data, click Total, origin. Origin means the country a person was born in, so this file counts people born in Tonga wherever they live now. A spreadsheet downloads; open the sheet called Table 1.

Now the part where you might get confused, because I did. Find your country’s row, and before you read anything look at the headings at the top of the sheet. The years 1990 to 2024 run three times across the page: the first block is both sexes together, the second is men, the third is women, and the heading that says which block you are in sits two rows above the years, so once you scroll to the right you see only a year. If you go straight to the last column you get the women’s figure and think it is the total. Go back to the first column headed 2024 for the total. For Tonga: 53,237 people abroad in 2024, of whom 28,839 are men and 24,398 are women.

That number means little on its own, so we need the number living at home, and it is on the site you already know. Open data.worldbank.org, type Population, total, click the line with that name, and click Tonga in the list under the chart: 104,175 people in 2024. Put the two together: for every 100 people living in Tonga, 51 people born in Tonga live abroad. For Jamaica it is 44 for every 100, and for the Comoros 42. The remittance figure on the last slide is sent by this group, so when a ministry reads that remittances are 39% of GDP, this is the size of the population behind that number.

Now the men and the women. From Tonga, more men are abroad than women, 28,839 against 24,398, and the seasonal work schemes in Australia and New Zealand, which recruit mostly men for fruit picking and meat packing, are part of the reason; we come back to those schemes this afternoon. From Jamaica and the Comoros, more women are abroad than men. Why should a ministry care which it is? Think about it for a moment. Here are two reasons to start with. Who is abroad decides who is missing at home: a village where the men are away has women running the farms and the households, and a village where the women are away has grandmothers raising the children. And the schemes that send men abroad are government policy, so a ministry that sees men leaving in their thousands is looking at the result of its own agreements.

What this file cannot tell you is who among the 53,237 sends money and who does not, or what the money pays for once it arrives. The count is of people abroad, not of senders. No national figure goes that far, which is why the FAR-SIDS household survey asks each household how many women and how many men outside the house sent money or goods in the last year, and who in the house received it. Write your four numbers down with their year, and keep them beside the remittance figure.

Part one · Where to find the figures · Demonstration 8 of 9

Your national household survey is the only source that counts how many households receive remittances, and the figure is one paragraph in a long report

How many households on your island receive remittances, and which households are they?

The reports list on the Tonga Statistics Department household survey page
Tonga Statistics Department, household survey reportsPlanning Institute of Jamaica, JSLC 2019 overviewINSEED Comoros, EHCVM 2024 results report
The clicks, in order
  1. For Tonga, open tongastats.gov.to. In the top menu choose Survey, then Household Income and Expenditure Survey. Scroll to HIES reports and click Download beside Tonga 2021 HIES Report. Every statistics office has a survey like this; the last slide of part one shows how to find yours.
  2. Open the PDF and search it for the word remittance. In a French speaking country search transfert, in a Portuguese speaking one remessa. The first hits are the contents pages; keep going to the first hit in the text itself. For Tonga that is printed page 21, section 1.2.3, one paragraph.
  3. Read that paragraph and the chart on the page after it, and write down three things: the percentage of households that received remittances (Tonga: 90%), the year the survey was carried out (Tonga: 2021, given on page xi), and the report’s own words for what it counted (Tonga: “cash remittances during the last 12 months”). Those words tell you whether money from inside the country was counted too. In Tonga it was.
  4. Write down every split the report gives beside the national figure. Tonga’s Figure 37 splits the 90% by island, by town and country, by whether a woman or a man heads the household, by the head’s age, by disability, and by the five spending groups from poorest to richest.
  5. If the full report is sold rather than free, as in Jamaica, download the free overview instead; the figure is in it. If your office publishes no report at all, the last slide of part one gives the other places to look.
What you should see

Share of households that received remittances, from each country’s own survey report.
