Tonga: 96% of households headed by a woman against 88% headed by a man; 94% in Vava’u against 64% in Ongo Niua (page 21 and Figure 37 of the 2021 report). Jamaica: 59.4% of households headed by a woman against 53.1% headed by a man; 63.6% in Kingston against 48.3% in other towns (page xii of the 2019 overview). The Comoros: the 2024 results report gives no single national share; its Figure 7 gives the share for each tenth of households from poorest to richest, and its text says the richest households are about 15 percentage points more likely to receive money from abroad than the poorest (page 10).

In all three countries the better off households receive more. In Tonga money from abroad makes up 22% of income in the poorest fifth of households and 40% in the richest fifth (page 49). In Jamaica 42.5% of the poorest fifth receive against 61.0% of the richest. In the Comoros the richest tenth of households receive about a quarter of all the money sent from abroad.

What this source cannot tell you. How much each household received, unless the report gives a value as well as a count, who inside the household received it, and who decided what to do with it. And no survey anywhere gives the matching figure for aid: there is no national count of households that received an aid programme.

Why this matters

This is the only figure in the whole day that counts households rather than dollars. For remittances it tells you how many households receive and which kinds: in Tonga nine in every ten, in Jamaica just over half, and in all three countries the better off households more often than the poorest. For aid there is no such figure anywhere, because donors count money paid and projects built, never the households a programme reached. Tomorrow’s map has a row called “who receives” for each flow, and this slide is the last source that can fill any part of it; the rest you fill from what you know about your own island.

Sources

Tonga Statistics Department. (2022). Tonga 2021 household income and expenditure survey report. Retrieved September 18, 2026, from https://tongastats.gov.to/survey/hies-survey/

Planning Institute of Jamaica and Statistical Institute of Jamaica. (2021). Jamaica survey of living conditions 2019: Overview. Retrieved September 20, 2026, from https://www.pioj.gov.jm/product/jamaica-survey-of-living-conditions-jslc-2019-overview/

Institut National de la Statistique et des Etudes Economiques et Démographiques. (2026). Principaux résultats de l’Enquête Harmonisée sur les Conditions de Vie des Ménages 2024. Retrieved September 20, 2026, from https://nada.inseed-comores.org/index.php/catalog/15/related-materials

Every source so far counts money crossing a border. This one counts households, and it is the only source in the day that does. Your assignment asks who receives and who decides, and it cannot begin without this figure.

I am doing it for Tonga; follow on your own laptop. Open tongastats.gov.to, choose Survey in the top menu, then Household Income and Expenditure Survey, scroll to HIES reports and click Download beside Tonga 2021 HIES Report. The file is 149 pages, and you need one of them. Search the PDF for the word remittance. The first hits are the contents pages; keep going to the first hit in the text itself, which is printed page 21, section 1.2.3, one paragraph. It says that 90% of households received cash remittances in the twelve months before the survey, that the highest shares were in Vava’u and rural Tongatapu and the lowest in Ongo Niua at 64%, and that 96% of households headed by a woman received against 88% headed by a man. Turn the page and Figure 37 gives the same 90% split every way the survey can split it: by island, by town and country, by the sex and the age of the head, by disability, and by the five spending groups from poorest to richest, where the poorest fifth is at 87% and the richest at 90%. The year the survey was in the field, January to November 2021, is on page xi.

Now the third thing to write down: the report’s own words for what it counted. Here they are “cash remittances during the last 12 months”. Nothing in that says from abroad. Figure 38 on page 22 confirms it: about a third of the money came from New Zealand, a third from Australia, and the rest from the United States, from elsewhere, and from inside Tonga, and households in Ongo Niua depended mostly on cash from other islands. So Tonga’s 90% is households receiving cash from anyone outside the house, at home or overseas. A student who writes “90% of Tongan households receive remittances from abroad” has misread the report. That is why you copy the words and not just the number, and it is the lesson of the three surveys slide this morning.

Your island may not publish a report like this, or may publish it differently, and the last slide of part one shows what I found when I looked for five other islands. For now, two of our own three. Jamaica sells its full survey report for 30 dollars, but the ten page overview is free on the Planning Institute’s site, and the figure is on its page xii: 55.9% of households received remittances in 2019, 63.6% in Kingston and 48.3% in the other towns, 42.5% of the poorest fifth of households against 61.0% of the richest, 59.4% of households headed by a woman against 53.1% headed by a man. The Comoros published a 17 page results report for its 2024 survey in May this year, in French, on the statistics office’s own data catalogue. It gives no single national share. Instead, its Figure 7 gives the share of people receiving money from abroad for each tenth of households from poorest to richest, and the text on page 10 says the richest households are about 15 percentage points more likely to receive than the poorest, and that the richest tenth of households receive about a quarter of all the money sent from abroad. So for the Comoros you write down the figure by spending group, say that the report gives no national total, and cite the page.

Put the three beside each other and one pattern appears in all of them. In Tonga money from abroad makes up 22% of income in the poorest fifth of households and 40% in the richest fifth. In Jamaica 42.5% of the poorest fifth receive against 61.0% of the richest. In the Comoros the richest tenth receive a quarter of the money. In every one of our three countries the better off households receive more, not less. Most people expect the opposite, so sit with two questions. First: if the poorest households receive the least from abroad, who is remittance money a safety net for, and who is left without one? Second: aid programmes usually choose their households by a rule, the poorest, the most exposed to cyclones, the ones without a water tank, while remittances arrive with a person and go where that person’s family is. Do the two flows reach the same households, or different ones? No survey in the world answers that today, because no survey asks about aid and remittances in the same house, and that is the question the FAR-SIDS household survey is built to ask.

What this report cannot tell you is how much each household received, who inside the house received it, or who decided what to do with it. And for aid there is no report like this anywhere: donors count money paid and projects built, and no statistics office counts the households an aid programme reached. Tomorrow’s map has a row for who receives each flow, and after this slide you have every public source there is for it. The rest of that row you fill from what you know about your own island, which is the point of the map.

Part one · Where to find the figures · Demonstration 9 of 9

The lender’s own project documents are the only place that says who a project was meant to reach and how many it reached

Behind one line of the aid total, who was the money for?

The project list for Jamaica on projects.worldbank.org
World Bank projects, JamaicaWorld Bank projects, all countriesAsian Development Bank projectsInter-American Development Bank projects
The clicks, in order
  1. Open projects.worldbank.org and click the Project List tab.
  2. Open Country in the filter panel on the left, choose your country and click Go.
  3. The table gives the project title, the identifier beginning with P, the commitment amount, the status and the approval date. Open a project whose title looks relevant to a livelihood: housing, social protection, water, schools.
  4. Inside the project, click the Documents tab.
  5. Open the Project Appraisal Document, written before the money is spent. It states who the project is for and how many people it should reach.
  6. Open the Implementation Completion Report, written afterwards, which says how many it actually reached. For a project funded elsewhere, the Asian Development Bank and the Inter-American Development Bank publish the same two documents.
What you should see

Jamaica has 161 World Bank projects listed. The most recent is the Hurricane Melissa Reconstruction Implementation Support Project, P515022, five million US dollars, approved 30 June 2026.

Tonga’s largest current project is the Sustainable Economic Corridors and Urban Resilience Project, P512750: an 80 million US dollar grant from the Asian Development Bank, a 40 million World Bank grant and 25 million from the Government of Tonga, for a bridge across the Fanga’uta lagoon with roads and drainage in Nuku’alofa.

This is the bridge into part two of today. The appraisal document is the only document in the whole day that names a target group, and even it names a number of people rather than a household.

What this source cannot tell you. Whether the people named as the target were the people reached. The completion report gives a count, and no document here follows a single household.

Why this matters

Every aid figure today counted money at the level of the country. These two documents, the appraisal document before the money is spent and the completion report after, are the only ones in the day that name the people a project was meant to reach and how many it reached. For the aid column of tomorrow’s map, this is where you read who a programme was for, and it is the closest any aid source comes to the “who receives” row that the household survey gives you for remittances.

Sources

World Bank. (n.d.). Projects & Operations. Retrieved September 18, 2026, from https://projects.worldbank.org/

Asian Development Bank. (n.d.). Projects. Retrieved September 18, 2026, from https://www.adb.org/projects

I am opening the World Bank project list for Jamaica, then the Hurricane Melissa reconstruction project, and going straight to the Documents tab, so you can see the appraisal document and the completion report sitting side by side.

Most of you have never seen one of these documents, so here is what they are. Before a lender releases money it writes an appraisal document, which argues why the project is needed, states who it is for, and commits to a number of people it will reach. Years later it writes a completion report, which says what happened. Both are public, both are long, and almost nobody outside the institution reads them.

These are the only documents in today’s whole list that name a group of people. Every figure we have opened until now counts dollars crossing a border. Hold that thought into part two, where the question becomes who decides.

You do not read the whole document. The appraisal document has a results framework near the front, usually a table, giving the indicators and the target numbers. The completion report has the same table with the achieved column filled in. Those two tables are the five minutes of reading that matter.

In your group, find one project on your own island and say, from its appraisal document, who the project names as its beneficiaries and whether a household like yours would be among them.

If a page has moved by the time you look, search World Bank projects and operations and use the Project List tab, then the Country filter. If your island is not one of our three, find out which bank lends to it and go to that bank’s project pages. The Asian Development Bank covers the Pacific, the Inter-American Development Bank and the Caribbean Development Bank cover the Caribbean, and the African Development Bank covers the Indian Ocean and Atlantic islands. All four publish appraisal and completion documents under the same two names.

Part one · Where to find the figures · The method for any island

The three figures exist for every small island state, and the places to look are the same everywhere

What do you do when the island you are writing about is not Tonga, Jamaica or the Comoros?

The balance of payments page of the Banque Centrale des Comores, the thinnest of our three cases
World Bank Open Data, all indicatorsOECD Data ExplorerPacific Data Hub Microdata LibraryWorld Bank Microdata Library
The clicks, in order
  1. Aid as a share of national income. One page on data.worldbank.org holds every country; find yours in the table under the chart.
  2. Who paid. The OECD Data Explorer, Recipient filter, and the Non-DAC branch of the same table.
  3. Who paid that the OECD misses. AidData for China, everywhere. The Lowy map if your island is in the Pacific.
  4. Remittances. Your central bank’s balance of payments, under Statistics, Economic Reviews or Publications; the line may be called personal transfers, workers’ remittances, secondary income or transferts courants. Then the World Bank page for the share of GDP.
  5. Households. Your statistics office’s site, for a survey called household income and expenditure, living conditions, household budget or integrated household; then the office’s data catalogue; then the regional library; then, last, the World Bank Microdata Library.
  6. When you find nothing. Write what you searched for, where and when, and put that in your map in place of the number.
What you should see

Every island keeps its household survey somewhere different. Fiji: on the statistics office site. Vanuatu: on the statistics office site, behind a Learn more button. Jamaica: a free overview on the Planning Institute’s site, and the full report costs 30 US dollars. The Comoros: on the statistics office’s own data catalogue. The Bahamas and St Vincent: in neither microdata library. The World Bank Microdata Library holds none of the household surveys of the 24 island states I checked, so it is the last place to look.

What this method cannot tell you. Who inside the household received the money and who decided what to do with it, which is why tomorrow you map it rather than look it up.

What each figure tells you, what it cannot, and where tomorrow’s map takes over
Sources

Fiji Bureau of Statistics. (2021). 2019-20 household income and expenditure survey. Retrieved September 20, 2026, from https://www.statsfiji.gov.fj/2019-20-hies/

Call out an island that is not one of our three, and I will find its aid share and its remittance share now, in front of you, using only this slide. It takes about ninety seconds.

The three worked cases were chosen for a reason. Tonga is the Pacific, Jamaica is the Caribbean, the Comoros is the Indian Ocean and it is also the case with the least published data. Between them they cover the three seas where small island developing states sit. The two sources that never fail are the World Bank indicator pages, because every country in the world is on them, and the OECD Data Explorer, because every aid recipient is in its Recipient filter. Start there, whatever your island. AidData covers China everywhere, and the Lowy map covers the Pacific only.

The two that need digging are the central bank and the household survey. For the central bank, search your country’s name with the words central bank, open the bank’s own site rather than a news article, and look for Statistics, Economic Reviews or Publications. For the household survey, I tried five other islands before today so that I could tell you what to expect, and each one was different. Fiji’s statistics office has the 2019 report on its site, but that report gives remittances as a share of income for each tenth of households and never says how many households receive. Vanuatu’s office lists its 2020 report behind a Learn more button. Jamaica’s figure is not on the statistics office site at all; it is in a free overview on the Planning Institute’s site, and the full report costs 30 dollars. The Comoros publishes on the statistics office’s own data catalogue, a separate site, in French. For the Bahamas and St Vincent I found nothing in either of the two big libraries. So the order is: search your country’s name with statistics office and look for a survey called household income and expenditure, living conditions, household budget or integrated household; then look on that office’s site for a page called data catalogue or microdata; then the regional library, which for the Pacific is microdata.pacificdata.org; and only then the World Bank Microdata Library. I checked that library for 24 island states, and it holds none of their household surveys, so it comes last, not first. Whatever you find, the classwork asks for a figure with its year, what it measures and where you found it. Old is fine. A PDF is fine. French is fine. Write down what you searched for and when, and if you found nothing, that sentence goes in your map in place of the number.

Now look at the diagram, because it is the bridge to tomorrow. Down the left are the three figures you can now find for any island. In the middle is what each one cannot tell you. On the right is the part of tomorrow’s map that takes over where the figure stops. The aid share and the donor table tell you how much aid arrived and from whom; they cannot tell you which programme reached which household, and the aid column of the map is where you name the programme. The remittance share tells you how much families sent; it cannot tell you which households received it, and the remittance column is where you name the channel. The household survey tells you how many households receive remittances and which kinds; it cannot tell you who inside the house received it or who decided, and for aid there is no household count at all. Those two questions, who receives and who decides, are the last two rows of the map, and you fill them from what you know about your own island, not from a source. That is the whole reason the map exists: the figures stop at the front door of the house, and the map goes inside.

Part two

A dollar of aid and a dollar from a relative are worth the same at the bank, and they stop being the same the moment somebody decides what they are for

Different people decide, they decide from different places, and the money arrives with different strings. Tonga is the worked example.

Who decides

The usual path each kind of money takes to a household, where the two paths differ, and the case where a government sits at the top of both.

What researchers find

When the two flows are compared in the same study they behave differently, in the economy and in the household, and the same flow behaves differently from one place to another.

Tonga in both accounts

The same country read from the national accounts, and then read from the household.

We have spent the first part of the afternoon on how the money is counted. Now we ask what happens once it has arrived. At the bank, a dollar of aid and a dollar sent by a sister in Auckland are identical. Inside an island they are not, and the reason is that different people decide what each dollar is for, and they decide from different places, under different conditions.

By different conditions I mean who chose the purpose, what the money can become once it is here, and what the receiver owes in return. An aid agency in Canberra or Brussels usually writes down what a grant is for before your government has seen it, whereas a sister in Auckland decides on the phone on a Sunday night, often with the household on the other end of the call. A water tank paid for by a donor stays a water tank, and it is very hard to turn it into school fees, whereas cash from a sister can become school fees on Monday and a roof repair after the next cyclone. An aid project usually asks your government for reports, audits and conditions, whereas a remittance carries obligations to the sender, to the church and to the family that no ministry can see, because they are never written down.

Before we go further, think about your own household. Think of the last money that came into it from outside: a wage, a scholarship, a government payment, a transfer from a relative. Who decided what it was for, and where was that person when they decided? Keep your answer, because I will ask you for it in a few minutes.

Tonga is the example I use through this part of the lecture, because Tonga receives both kinds of money on a large scale, and because the data allow us to look at the same country from the national accounts and from inside the household.

Part two · Who decides

In one common case, aid passes through about six decisions before it reaches a household, and a remittance through two

The shaded steps are where the household enters. In the aid path the decisions are recorded in documents and made a long way from the household. In the remittance path they are made between family members and recorded nowhere a ministry can read, which is why a household survey, and not the national accounts, is where you learn what a remittance was for.

A question for you

At which step of the aid path does anybody ask the household what it needs? And in your own family, who has the last word on what a remittance is for, the person who sent it or the person who received it, and does that change when the amount is large?

Sources

World Bank. (n.d.). Remittance Prices Worldwide: New Zealand to Tonga [Data set]. Retrieved September 17, 2026, from https://remittanceprices.worldbank.org/corridor/New-Zealand/Tonga

The two paths on the screen are one common case each, and I want you to treat them as examples rather than as rules. In the aid path, a donor parliament in Canberra, Wellington or Brussels votes the budget, the aid agency chooses countries and sectors, your government negotiates the project and often puts in money of its own, the project team writes the rule for who takes part, some households fit the rule and some do not, and the household that fits usually receives a service rather than cash: a tank, a clinic, a fee waiver, or in a growing number of programmes a payment with a condition attached, such as keeping a child in school.

That is a project, and aid does not always arrive as a project. When a donor gives budget support, the money goes straight into your government's general budget, there is no project team and no selection rule, and the household never knows which road or which nurse the donor paid for. When aid arrives as a scholarship, the household is chosen by an exam and receives something close to cash. When it arrives after a cyclone, the negotiation is skipped, the money comes in weeks, and it comes as tarpaulins and rice. So the six steps are the usual path for a project, and the number of steps can be four or eight depending on the form the aid takes.

Now the remittance path. A relative abroad earns the money and decides how much to send and what for, and I say decides with the household because in most families I know that decision is a phone call, not an order. The money travels, and on the World Bank's Remittance Prices Worldwide series the transfer company took about 8 dollars in every 100 on the New Zealand to Tonga corridor in late 2025. Then the household receives it, and sender and receiver settle between them what it pays for.

That too is one case. The sender is not always abroad; a brother in Nuku'alofa sending money to Ha'apai is a remittance to that household, and it never appears in the national figure. The money does not always pass through a company; a seasonal worker who flies home in October with cash in his bag has remitted, and the national accounts never see it. And the household does not always decide: when a sister sends money marked for the school fee, or pays the school directly, or sends the misinale contribution for the church, the purpose was fixed before the money arrived. Remittances arrive with strings too. The difference is who tied the string and how far away they were standing when they tied it.

So, the first question. At which step of the aid path does anybody ask the household what it needs? Look at the chain and find it. In many projects the honest answer is the fourth step at the earliest, when the selection rule is written, and in some projects the answer is nowhere. Now the second question, and I want real answers from your own families. Who has the last word on what a remittance is for, the person who sent it or the person who received it? And does the answer change when the amount is large, when it is a roof rather than a phone top-up? I ask because my own research rests on that question, and what I have found so far is that the answer differs from family to family and from island to island.

Part two · When a government decides the remittance too

Some remittances exist because a government decided they should, and the money is still counted as private

Is the scheme aid?The scheme is aid only in part. For the New Zealand scheme the OECD counts the workers’ training as aid and excludes the cost of running the scheme, because the scheme is there to fill labour shortages in New Zealand. For tomorrowAsk which of your island's remittance flows exist because of a government policy. Tonga's central bank has counted seasonal earnings within remittances since 2014, and they reached a tenth of the total by 2025.
Sources

OECD Development Assistance Committee. (2023). ODA casebook on activities in the field of migration (DCD/DAC/STAT(2023)34/FINAL). OECD. https://one.oecd.org/document/DCD/DAC/STAT(2023)34/FINAL/en/pdf

New Zealand Government. (2024, August 14). RSE scheme revitalised and cap increased [Press release]. https://www.beehive.govt.nz/release/rse-scheme-revitalised-and-cap-increased

Department of Employment and Workplace Relations. (2026). PALM scheme data publication, June 2026 [Data set]. Pacific Australia Labour Mobility scheme. https://www.palmscheme.gov.au/

Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment. (2026). Migration data explorer: Visa holder population by nationality and visa type [Data set]. Retrieved September 17, 2026, from https://www.mbie.govt.nz/immigration-and-tourism/immigration/migration-research-and-evaluation/migration-data-explorer

1News. (2026, August 2). Seasonal work in NZ helping Tongans build businesses back home. https://www.1news.co.nz/2026/08/02/seasonal-work-in-nz-helping-tongans-build-businesses-back-home/

On the last slide one path had a government at the top and the other had a family. In the Pacific, one of the largest remittance flows has a government at the top as well. Wellington sets the number of places, a Tongan worker earns the money, his family receives it, and the central bank counts it as a private transfer. Labour schemes are where the two kinds of money meet. New Zealand's Recognised Seasonal Employer scheme, capped at 20,750 places a year since August 2024, and Australia's Pacific Australia Labour Mobility scheme, known as PALM, bring Pacific workers to seasonal jobs such as picking fruit and packing meat, and they produce a large remittance flow by design. On 30 June 2026, 3,715 Tongans held PALM visas in Australia, 3,095 of them men, and on the same day 798 Tongans held New Zealand seasonal work visas, 729 of them men; New Zealand's season peaks in March, when 1,311 Tongans held them (MBIE, 2026). Both figures count people holding a visa on one day, so they can stand side by side. A journalist estimates that the two schemes together employ about one in five working Tongan men, and the screen shows that figure as an estimate.

A donor government therefore designs a labour scheme, the scheme produces remittances, and the remittances are counted as private transfers. The OECD has ruled on both schemes in its casebook. For the New Zealand scheme it counts the workers’ training programme as aid and excludes the cost of running the scheme, because employers must first show that they cannot fill the job locally, so the scheme is there to fill labour shortages in New Zealand. For the Australian scheme it counts the part the aid ministry pays for, and it states that migrants sending money home is not on its own enough to make a programme aid (OECD DAC, 2023). Thus the schemes are immigration policy with a small aid component, and they produce a private flow that barely appears in the aid statistics of the country that designed them. For tomorrow, ask which of your island's remittance flows exist because of a government policy. Jamaica has its own example, the Overseas Employment Programme, which sends workers to Canada and the United States.

Part two · What researchers find when they compare the two flows

When aid and remittances are compared in the same study they behave differently, and the same flow behaves differently from one place to another

Few studies put both flows into one model. Two results, on prices and on spending.

The real exchange rate, and Dutch diseaseThe price of what your island produces compared with the same goods abroad. A large aid project brings US dollars to Tonga; to be spent they become pa'anga and chase the same builders, drivers and land, so prices and wages rise and the pa'anga strengthens, and a squash farmer selling to Japan has higher costs at home and a dearer price abroad. Economists call that Dutch disease, after the Netherlands in the 1960s.
Why the place mattersIn the island study families spent remittances largely on imported goods, paid for abroad, which do not chase Tongan builders. In Latin America families spent more of the money on housing and services at home, which do. What decides the effect is who spends the money and on what, not the name of the flow.
A question for you

If your government receives 50 million next year for a new hospital, and families on your island receive 50 million from relatives in the same year, which of the two would you expect to raise the wage of a builder in your capital, and why?

Sources

Amuedo-Dorantes, C., & Pozo, S. (2004). Workers' remittances and the real exchange rate: A paradox of gifts. World Development, 32(8), 1407–1417. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.worlddev.2004.02.004

Amuedo-Dorantes, C., Pozo, S., & Vargas-Silva, C. (2007). Remittances and the macroeconomy: The case of small island developing states (WIDER Research Paper No. 2007/22). UNU-WIDER. https://www.wider.unu.edu/sites/default/files/rp2007-22.pdf

Acosta, P. A., Lartey, E. K. K., & Mandelman, F. S. (2009). Remittances and the Dutch disease. Journal of International Economics, 79(1), 102–116. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jinteco.2009.06.007

Rajan, R. G., & Subramanian, A. (2011). Aid, Dutch disease, and manufacturing growth. Journal of Development Economics, 94(1), 106–118. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jdeveco.2009.12.004

Werker, E., Ahmed, F. Z., & Cohen, C. (2009). How is foreign aid spent? Evidence from a natural experiment. American Economic Journal: Macroeconomics, 1(2), 225–244. https://doi.org/10.1257/mac.1.2.225

We have followed each kind of money to the household. Now I want to show you what happens when researchers put the two flows side by side, first in the economy as a whole and then, on the next slides, inside the house. Very few studies do this. Most study one flow and treat the other as background, so the results I am about to show you come from a handful of papers, and I will tell you where each one was done, because the place turns out to matter.

The first result is about prices, and the measure is the real exchange rate: the price of what your island produces compared with the price of the same goods abroad. Let me explain it with an example. A large aid project arrives in Tonga and brings US dollars. To spend them in Tonga, the dollars have to be changed into pa'anga and spent on Tongan things: builders, drivers, office staff, land, rent. The island has only so many builders and so much land, so when a lot of new money chases the same builders and the same plots, their prices and wages go up. At the same time, all those dollars being changed into pa'anga make the pa'anga stronger. Now think of a farmer who sells squash to Japan, or a hotel that sells rooms to Australians. Their costs at home have gone up, and a foreign buyer needs more dollars to pay the same price in pa'anga, so their squash and their rooms have become dearer abroad and they sell less. Economists call this Dutch disease, after what happened in the Netherlands when income from natural gas arrived in the 1960s.

Now look at the rows. Across nineteen small island states, aid produced this effect and remittances did not (Amuedo-Dorantes, Pozo and Vargas-Silva, 2007). If I stopped there you would leave thinking remittances are safe and aid is dangerous, and that would be wrong, because across thirteen Latin American countries remittances did raise the real exchange rate (Amuedo-Dorantes and Pozo, 2004), and across many countries aid raised it and the industries that export grew more slowly (Rajan and Subramanian, 2011). Why the difference between the islands and Latin America? The most likely answer is what the money was spent on. In the island study, families spent remittances largely on imported goods, a fridge from Auckland, a motorbike, rice, which are paid for abroad and do not chase the island's builders and land. In Latin America families spent more of the money on housing and services at home, which do. So the lesson is not that one flow is harmless and the other harmful. The lesson is that the effect depends on who spends the money and on what, and that is a question about your island, not about the name of the flow.

The second result is about spending, and it comes from a clever piece of research. When the price of oil rises, the Gulf governments earn more and give more aid to poorer Muslim countries, and because the oil price is set on world markets, nobody in those countries decides how much aid they receive. Werker, Ahmed and Cohen (2009) used that to follow what happened to the money. Most of it was consumed rather than invested, largely on imported goods, it replaced saving at home rather than adding to it, and it had no measurable effect on prices or on growth. Then they noticed something that matters for us. When oil prices rise, the families of Gulf workers also send more money home, at the same time and to the same countries. Once they counted those remittances, up to a third of what had looked like the effect of aid on consumption and imports turned out to be money families had sent. A study that leaves one flow out will credit the other with what families paid for, and that is one more reason this module keeps the two flows apart.

So here is my question, and I want you to answer it for your own island. If your government receives 50 million next year for a new hospital, and families on your island receive 50 million from relatives in the same year, which of the two would you expect to raise the wage of a builder in your capital, and why? Think about who spends each 50 million and what they spend it on.

Part two · What the money pays for

Tongan households that received more remittances earned more from business, and Fijian households did not

A coefficientThe number a statistical model gives for how much one thing changes when another rises by one. Here, for every extra dollar of remittances a Tongan household received, its business income was on average 52 cents higher.
What it does not showThe result is an association measured at one point in time, and the authors state that it does not prove the dollar caused the business. They explain the difference between Tonga and Fiji by the age of the migration corridor.
Sources

Brown, R. P. C., & Leeves, G. (2011). Comparative effects of migrants’ remittances on composition of recipient household income in two small, island economies. Applied Economics, 43(27), 3965–3976. https://doi.org/10.1080/00036841003742611

Those were results for whole economies. The next three slides go inside the house, and they start with what the money pays for once it arrives. Brown and Leeves, reading 2, asked the same questions in the same year in Tonga and in Fiji to find out what remittances pay for once they arrive. They report the answer as a coefficient, which is the number a statistical model gives for how much one thing changes when another rises by one. In Tonga the coefficient on business income was 0.52, which means that for every extra dollar of remittances a household received, its business income was on average 52 cents higher. In Fiji there was no such effect, and the only consistent result was lower wage income, meaning that people worked fewer paid hours (Brown and Leeves, 2011, Table 6).

The result is an association measured at one point in time, and the authors state that it does not prove the dollar caused the business. They explain the difference by the age of the migration corridor. Tongans have migrated regularly for four decades, so families can plan around the money and invest part of it, whereas migration from Fiji is more recent and the money arrives less predictably. For a ministry, this means that how long the money has been arriving and how regularly it comes matter as much as the amount.

Part two · What the money pays for

In rural Samoa, households spent 29 dollars of every 100 received from abroad on customary obligations and church giving

Fa'alavelaveThe Samoan term for customary obligations such as weddings, funerals, elections and titles. It took 17 dollars of every 100 received, before any ordinary spending.
MisinaleThe annual church donation in Tonga. About a third of remittance transactions are at least partly intended for it, and one study had to report household income twice, with and without those transfers.
KavengaThe Tongan term for obligation in general: the duties a household owes to kin, church and community. Meeting them maintains a household's standing and its right to call on others in a crisis.
What is not measuredNo published wellbeing indicator records this spending, and nobody has yet measured what share of Tongan household income goes to kavenga and misinale.
Sources

Le Dé, L., Gaillard, J. C., Friesen, W., & Matautia Smith, F. (2015). Remittances in the face of disasters: A case study of rural Samoa. Environment, Development and Sustainability, 17(3), 653–672. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10668-014-9559-0

McKenzie, D., Gibson, J., & Stillman, S. (2007). Moving to opportunity, leaving behind what? Evaluating the initial effects of a migration policy on incomes and poverty in source areas. New Zealand Economic Papers, 41(2), 197–223. https://doi.org/10.1080/00779950709558509

Le Dé and colleagues, reading 4, found that in rural Samoa before the 2009 tsunami the largest single use of remittances was neither food nor housing. Households spent about 17 dollars of every 100 received on fa'alavelave, the customary obligations of weddings, funerals, elections and titles, and about 12 dollars on church donations, so 29 dollars of every 100 went to obligations before any ordinary spending, while small business received 3 (Le Dé et al., 2015, p. 664). In Tonga the annual church donation is the misinale, and about a third of remittance transactions are at least partly intended for it, so one study had to report household income twice, once with those transfers and once without them (McKenzie, Gibson and Stillman, 2007, p. 207). Kavenga is the Tongan term for obligation in general, meaning the duties a household owes to kin, church and community. What is the word on your own island? Most islands have one, and I would like to hear yours.

This spending should not be read as waste, because kavenga and misinale maintain a household's standing and its right to call on others when something goes wrong, and in a country with almost no formal insurance, that standing is what a household relies on in a crisis. However, the spending is invisible in the official figures, because no published wellbeing indicator records it and nobody has yet measured what share of Tongan household income goes to it. A household survey could measure it, and we return to that possibility in part three.

Part two · What the migrant no longer contributes

A household with a migrant gains the remittances and loses the migrant's work at home, and many calculations count only the gain

The simple methodTake the household's income, subtract the remittances, and call the difference the gain from migration. The method assumes that the person who left would have earned nothing at home.
The counterfactualThe economists' term for what would have happened otherwise: what the migrant would have earned, grown and cared for if they had stayed. Once it is counted, the measured fall in poverty in Latin America shrinks from 14% to 3%.
A migration lottery as evidenceNew Zealand ran a ballot for Tongan migration, so chance decided who left. The families who lost the ballot are therefore a fair comparison, and in the first year the migrants' families had lower total income than they did.
Sources

Acosta, P., Calderón, C., Fajnzylber, P., & López, H. (2008). What is the impact of international remittances on poverty and inequality in Latin America? World Development, 36(1), 89–114. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.worlddev.2007.02.016

McKenzie, D., Gibson, J., & Stillman, S. (2007). Moving to opportunity, leaving behind what? Evaluating the initial effects of a migration policy on incomes and poverty in source areas. New Zealand Economic Papers, 41(2), 197–223. https://doi.org/10.1080/00779950709558509

Gibson, J., McKenzie, D., & Stillman, S. (2011). The impacts of international migration on remaining household members: Omnibus results from a migration lottery program. The Review of Economics and Statistics, 93(4), 1297–1318. https://doi.org/10.1162/REST_a_00129

Gibson, J., McKenzie, D., & Stillman, S. (2013). Accounting for selectivity and duration-dependent heterogeneity when estimating the impact of emigration on incomes and poverty in sending areas. Economic Development and Cultural Change, 61(2), 247–280. https://doi.org/10.1086/668276

When a son moves to Auckland and sends money home, the household gains the money and loses the son, meaning his wages, his work on the family plantation and his care for his parents. The simple method takes the household's income, subtracts the remittances, and calls the difference the gain from migration, which assumes that the son would have earned nothing if he had stayed.

Economists call the missing element the counterfactual, meaning what would have happened otherwise. Acosta and colleagues calculated the effect both ways for Latin America: when the migrant's lost earnings are ignored, migration reduces extreme poverty by about 14%, and when they are counted, the reduction is about 3%. For Mexico the direction reverses, so that once lost earnings are counted, migration is measured as increasing poverty (Acosta et al., 2008, Table 9).

The Tongan evidence is unusually strong, because New Zealand ran a ballot for Tongan migration and chance decided who left, so the families who lost the ballot are a fair comparison for the families of those who won. In the first year, the winners' families had lower total income, lower earnings, lower farm and business income and less food grown at home, and the remittances did not make up the loss (McKenzie, Gibson and Stillman, 2007). A later paper by the same authors on the Samoan ballot found the opposite result, poverty falling among the families left behind, with signs that the gain faded the longer the migrant had been away (Gibson, McKenzie and Stillman, 2013), so the answer differs by country and by how long the migrant has been away. Before crediting a remittance to a household, ask what the person who sent it would have earned, grown and cared for if they had stayed.

Part two · Tonga in the national accounts and in the household

The national accounts and the household account describe Tonga differently, and both rest on accurate figures

The national accounts show
  • Remittances equal about 39% of GDP: 38.6% in 2023 and 34.1% in 2024 on the National Reserve Bank of Tonga series, among the highest shares in the world.
  • Net aid equalled 20% of gross national income in 2023 and 51% in 2022, the year of the eruption.
  • Development assistance funded 51% of the national budget in 2023 to 2024.
  • Tonga is classed as upper middle income by income per person, and it has not been classed as a least developed country.
The household account shows
  • The person who earns the transfer is absent, and the household has lost their wages and the food they grew.
  • In rural Samoa, 29 dollars of every 100 received paid customary and church obligations before anything else; nobody has measured the Tongan share.
  • In the year to June 2025, Tonga paid 17.7 million US dollars to one creditor, out of 29.4 million in debt repayments, against an infrastructure budget of about 10.1 million.
  • On income per person Tonga would have lost its access to World Bank grants; it keeps them only through the exception the Bank makes for small island economies.
A claim for discussion

An income measure can record a gain in a country where a fuller account of the household records a loss.

The FAR-SIDS website: Tonga

On the FAR-SIDS website there is a page for Tonga that shows both flows over time, and I am opening it now. What follows is a claim for you to argue with, not a settled fact. The left card shows what a ministry of finance or a donor reads. Remittances equal about 39% of GDP, 38.6% in 2023 and 34.1% in 2024 on the National Reserve Bank of Tonga series, among the highest shares in the world, net aid equalled a fifth of national income in 2023 and half of it in the year of the eruption, development assistance funded about half of the national budget, and Tonga is classed as upper middle income by income per person and has not been classed as a least developed country. On these figures, Tonga is one of the most supported small economies in the world.

The right card shows what parts one and two have added. The person who earns the transfer is absent, and the household has lost their wages and the food they grew. In rural Samoa, 29 dollars of every 100 received paid obligations before anything else, and nobody has measured the Tongan share. In the year to June 2025 Tonga paid 17.7 million US dollars to one creditor, out of 29.4 million in debt repayments, against an infrastructure budget of about 10.1 million. In addition, on income per person alone Tonga would have lost its access to World Bank grants, the money you saw in the IDA row this afternoon, and it keeps that access only through the exception the Bank makes for small island economies, a process called graduation that reading 1, the State of SIDS Report summary, sets out. The claim is that an income measure can record a gain in a country where a fuller account of the household records a loss. I want you to disagree with this. The strongest objection is that the right card was chosen to make the point, and if that is your objection, make it, because it is a fair one.

Part three

From the national figure to the household, and what a ministry can do with what it finds

A national total records how much money arrived. The Sustainable Livelihoods Framework describes what that money meant for households, and your assignment asks you to apply it to your own island.

Why a total is not enough

What the money paid for, who in the house decided, and what the household had to survive.

The framework

Five assets, who controls each of them, and the conditions the household lives in.

What a ministry can do

The four tests a recommendation meets before it is worth writing.

In part two you saw that the same country can look supported in the national accounts and stretched inside the household, and that the difference comes down to who received the money and who decided what it was for. Part three gives you a tool for asking those two questions in an orderly way. A national total records how much money arrived, and the Sustainable Livelihoods Framework is the tool that describes what that money meant for the households that received it. Everything in this part is a tool you will use tomorrow and in your assignment, and I will introduce the framework through one worked example.

Part three · Why a framework is needed

A national total cannot show what the money paid for, who in the house decided, or what shock it had to cover

What it paid for

Which part of life did the money pay for?

A dollar spent on school fees, a dollar spent on a funeral and a dollar spent on a roof are the same dollar in the accounts and three different outcomes for a family.

Who decided

Who inside the house decided?

The money arrives with a person, that person's standing in the family shapes where it goes, and no account records who they were.

What it had to cover

What did the household have to survive?

After a cyclone, money that would have paid school fees pays for a roof. The household is no better off than before, although the figures may show more spending.

A national total cannot answer three questions that matter for a household. The first is which part of life the money paid for, because a dollar spent on school fees, a dollar spent on a funeral and a dollar spent on a roof are the same dollar in the accounts and three different outcomes for a family. The second is who inside the house decided, because the money arrives with a person, that person's standing in the family shapes where it goes, and no account records who they were.

The third is what the household had to survive. After a cyclone, a transfer that would have paid school fees pays for a roof, so the household is no better off than before, although the figures may show more spending. This question distinguishes the framework from a poverty line, because after a disaster a household can spend more than before and still be worse off, since it is replacing what it lost. These are not Pacific questions. A Maltese family in the 1960s with a brother in Australia faced all three: whether his money paid for a child's schooling or a wedding, whether the mother or the grandfather decided, and whether it went to rebuild after a bad year. The three questions correspond to the three parts of the framework on the next two slides.

Part three · The framework, first part

The Sustainable Livelihoods Framework starts from the five assets a household uses to make a living

Human

Health, schooling and skills

These give a household its capacity to work.

Social

Networks, church, kin and the obligations that go with them

These are the people who help when a household cannot manage alone, and the standing that kavenga and misinale maintain.

Physical

House, boat, tools, road and water tank

These are the things the household owns and uses.

Financial

Cash, savings and credit

The transfer itself belongs here.

Natural

Land, reef, soil and water

These are what the island provides.

The frameworkA way of describing a household's life in three parts: the assets it has to work with, who controls each asset, and the conditions around them. The British aid ministry developed it in 1999 with these five assets (DFID, 1999). Natarajan and colleagues (2022), reading 3, keep only financial and physical assets at the centre and place two further parts beside them: relational power, meaning who controls each asset, and the climate and environment around the household. This module teaches all five assets, with those two parts added.
TomorrowEach of the five assets is a row of your map, with a column for remittances and a column for aid. In each cell you name the programme or channel through which that flow reaches the asset.
Sources

Department for International Development. (1999). Sustainable livelihoods guidance sheets. https://www.livelihoodscentre.org/documents/114097690/114438878/Sustainable+livelihoods+guidance+sheets.pdf

Natarajan, N., Newsham, A., Rigg, J., & Suhardiman, D. (2022). A sustainable livelihoods framework for the 21st century. World Development, 155, Article 105898. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.worlddev.2022.105898

The Sustainable Livelihoods Framework describes a household's life in three parts: what it has to work with, who controls each of those things, and the conditions around them. The framework calls the things a household works with capitals, and I will call them assets. The British aid ministry developed the framework in 1999 with these five assets, and the 2022 revision on your reading list, by Natarajan and colleagues, keeps only financial and physical assets at the centre and places two further parts beside them, relational power, meaning who controls each asset, and the climate and environment the household lives in. They drop the other three because they argue that calling health, kinship and land forms of capital accepts a market reading of a household’s life. This module teaches all five assets, because you need all five to see what a transfer touches, and it adds the two parts the 2022 paper proposes. Those two parts are the next slide.

Human assets are health, schooling and skills, meaning the capacity to work. Social assets are networks, church and kin, the people who help when you cannot manage alone, together with the obligations that keep a household in good standing with them, which is where kavenga and the misinale belong. Physical assets are the house, boat, tools, road and water tank. Financial assets are cash, savings and credit, including the transfer itself, and natural assets are land, reef, soil and water. Give me one example of each of the five from your own island before we move on. Tomorrow each of these five assets becomes a row of your map, with one column for remittances and one for aid, and in each cell you name the programme or channel through which that flow reaches the asset. In the Jamaica example you will see tomorrow, remittances reach everyday human and social life, where aid is weakest, and aid reaches roads and water, where remittances cannot, and that pattern follows from who decides each flow.

Part three · The framework, second and third parts

The framework then asks who controls each asset and under what conditions, and gender enters both questions

Who decides

Receiving and controlling differ

The question is who could spend the transfer without asking anyone, which is not always the person it was addressed to.

Who is left out

Aid selection also involves power

Across 8,062 donor appraisals, Pacific projects scored about 0.15 lower on the donors' six point scale, which Wood, Otor and Dornan (2022) attribute to distance and small size rather than to weak government.

Relational powerThe term Natarajan and colleagues (2022) use for who controls each asset. Class, gender, age, rank in the family and political connection decide who receives, who is chosen for a programme, who spends and who is left out. Ask it of both flows.
The conditions, in one exampleA cyclone destroys the house (physical), damages the land (natural), calls on church and kin (social), and forces the cash (financial) to replace what was lost. Who holds the money then decides whether what remains pays school fees (human) or a church obligation (social).
Sources

Natarajan, N., Newsham, A., Rigg, J., & Suhardiman, D. (2022). A sustainable livelihoods framework for the 21st century. World Development, 155, Article 105898. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.worlddev.2022.105898

Department of Employment and Workplace Relations. (2026). PALM scheme data publication, June 2026 [Data set]. Pacific Australia Labour Mobility scheme. https://www.palmscheme.gov.au/

Bank of Jamaica. (2011). Remittances to Jamaica: Findings from a national survey of remittance recipients. https://www.boj.org.jm/uploads/pdf/papers_pamphlets/papers_pamphlets_Remittances_to_Jamaica_-_Findings_from_a_National_Survey_of_Remittance_Recipients.pdf

Wood, T., Otor, S., & Dornan, M. (2022). Why are aid projects less effective in the Pacific? Development Policy Review, 40(3), Article e12573. https://doi.org/10.1111/dpr.12573

The second part of the framework asks who controls each asset, which Natarajan and colleagues call relational power: class, gender, age, rank in the family and political connection decide who receives, who is chosen for a programme, who spends and who is left out, and the question applies to both flows. Gender is a question inside every part of the framework rather than a separate part, and it takes four concrete forms here. Of the 3,715 Tongans on PALM visas in June 2026, 3,095 were men, because the fruit picking corridors recruit men, while care and nursing corridors recruit more women, so the type of work decides who is absent from the household. In Jamaica's national survey of 2,072 remittance recipients, three in four were women (Bank of Jamaica, 2011), and that survey dates from 2010, so a Jamaican student can record that the latest national evidence on who receives is fifteen years old. Receiving and controlling also differ, so the useful question is who could spend the transfer without asking anyone, rather than to whom it was addressed. On the aid side, donors score their own projects, and across 8,062 appraisals Pacific projects scored about 0.15 lower on the donors' six point scale, which is the scale a donor uses to rate its own project from failure to full success, because the islands are distant and small rather than badly governed (Wood, Otor and Dornan, 2022), so being hard to reach is itself a disadvantage in who is chosen.

The third part is the conditions around all of this, and one example shows how they work. A cyclone destroys the house, which is a physical asset, damages the land, which is natural, calls on church and kin, which are social, and forces the cash, which is financial, to replace what was lost. Who holds the money then decides whether what remains pays school fees, a human asset, or a church obligation, a social one, so a single transfer touches all five assets, and who controls the money decides where it goes. Natarajan and colleagues call these two parts relational power and the climate and environment context, and they place them beside the assets rather than underneath them.

Part three · The indicators ministries publish

The indicators your ministry already publishes cannot show who received the money or who decided how to spend it

GDP per person

Output divided by population

It counts the transfer when it arrives, and it does not count the migrant's lost wages.

Poverty headcount

Share of people below a poverty line

A remittance that lifts one household just over the line and does nothing for another shows as a single change.

Human Development Index

Income, schooling and life expectancy combined

It records nothing on who inside the household received anything.

Multidimensional Poverty Index

Ten deprivations in health, education and living standards

It comes closer to the assets, and it still records neither obligation payments nor who decides.

Food Insecurity Experience Scale

Eight questions on running short of food

It records how severe the shortage was. The Kingston study used a scale of the same kind and found the effect of remittances there.

Gini coefficient

Inequality across households in one number

It cannot distinguish a country where remittances reach the poor from one where they reach the middle.

An indicatorOne measure published for every country every year. These six are the indicators most small island governments report, and each measures something well. None was designed to show a transfer arriving with a person.
Question three of the assignmentWhich indicators should the ministry monitor, and why do the ones it uses now fail to answer the question? This list is the starting point for your argument.
Sources

World Bank. (n.d.). GDP per capita (current US$) (NY.GDP.PCAP.CD) [Data set]. World Development Indicators. Retrieved September 17, 2026, from https://data.worldbank.org/indicator/NY.GDP.PCAP.CD

World Bank. (n.d.). Poverty headcount ratio at national poverty lines (% of population) (SI.POV.NAHC) [Data set]. World Development Indicators. Retrieved September 17, 2026, from https://data.worldbank.org/indicator/SI.POV.NAHC

World Bank. (n.d.). Gini index (SI.POV.GINI) [Data set]. World Development Indicators. Retrieved September 17, 2026, from https://data.worldbank.org/indicator/SI.POV.GINI

United Nations Development Programme. (n.d.). Human Development Index. Human Development Reports. Retrieved September 17, 2026, from https://hdr.undp.org/data-center/human-development-index

Oxford Poverty and Human Development Initiative & United Nations Development Programme. (2025). Global multidimensional poverty index 2025: Overlapping hardships, poverty and climate hazards. https://ophi.org.uk/global-mpi

Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations. (n.d.). Food Insecurity Experience Scale. Retrieved September 17, 2026, from https://www.fao.org/in-action/voices-of-the-hungry/fies/en/

Thomas-Hope, E. (2025). Migrant remittances, food security and inclusive social development in Jamaica. In J. Crush, A. Chikanda, & S. Ramachandran (Eds.), New directions in South-South migration (pp. 63–82). Springer. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-981-97-9715-8_4

Question three of your assignment asks which indicators the ministry should monitor and why the ones it uses now do not answer the question. These six are the ones most small island governments publish. GDP per person, which is output divided by population, counts the transfer when it arrives and does not count the migrant's lost wages at all. The poverty headcount, the share of people below a poverty line, shows a remittance that lifts one household just over the line and does nothing for another as a single change. The Human Development Index combines income, schooling and life expectancy into one number a year and records nothing on who inside the household received anything. The Multidimensional Poverty Index counts ten deprivations across health, education and living standards, so it comes closer to the assets, and it still records neither obligation payments nor who decides.

The Food Insecurity Experience Scale asks eight questions on whether the household ran short of food and records how severe the shortage was. In Kingston, Thomas-Hope (2025) asked the questions of a scale of the same kind, the Household Food Insecurity Access Scale, and found that households receiving remittances were no less likely to run short of food, while among poor households the shortage was less severe, so a measure that recorded only yes or no would have reported no effect where there was one. Finally, the Gini coefficient expresses inequality across households in one number, and it cannot distinguish a country where remittances reach the poor from one where they reach the middle. Each of these indicators measures something well, and none was designed to show a transfer arriving with a person, so in question three you argue which of them your own ministry should keep, which it should add to, and why.

Part three · A recommendation a ministry can act on

A recommendation that a ministry can act on meets four tests, and the assignment is marked against them

  1. An existing instrument to deliver it, such as a household survey already in the field or a ministry that already publishes the figure.
  2. A cost the budget can bear, stated against the fiscal position you described in your first question.
  3. A question the government is already asking, so that somebody wants the answer.
  4. A plain statement of what it will not do. A change in measurement does not change how much money arrives.
The Jamaica model answer on the VLE

About fifteen questions added to a survey already in the field

Add about fifteen questions on remittances to the Survey of Living Conditions, which the statistics office already runs: cash, goods and bills paid separately, who receives, how regularly, and what leaves the household again. The questions are cheap to add, and they answer a question the government asked after Hurricane Melissa, namely which households already have a private safety net.

The standard

Make one recommendation and argue it against all four tests, because five recommendations cannot each be argued properly in the space you have.

Question four of your assignment asks for one recommendation, argued against four tests. The recommendation needs an existing instrument to deliver it, such as a household survey already in the field or a ministry that already publishes the figure. It needs a cost the budget can bear, stated against the fiscal position you described in question one, and it needs to answer a question the government is already asking, so that somebody wants the answer. Finally, it needs a plain statement of what it will not do.

The Jamaica model answer on the VLE proposes one change in measurement: about fifteen questions added to the Survey of Living Conditions, which the statistics office already runs. The questions ask about cash, goods and bills paid separately, following the lesson of the Tongan surveys, about who receives, about how regularly the money comes, because a regular flow can fund a business, and about what leaves the household again as church and community giving. The change is cheap, it uses an instrument already in the field, and it answers a question the Jamaican government asked after Hurricane Melissa, namely which households already have a private safety net. Its last paragraph states that it will not change how much money arrives. Make one recommendation and argue it well, because five recommendations cannot each be argued against four tests in the space the assignment gives you.

Session two · A completed example

The Jamaica model answer shows the level of detail expected in each cell, and it records what the writer could not find

Human assets, remittances

School fees, uniforms, books and lunch money

Relatives send this money monthly and often earmark it, and they also pay private health costs when the public system cannot cope. The writer names a cousin's exam fees paid from Florida as her own experience.

Human assets, aid

PATH, and education loans

PATH, the government's conditional cash transfer, pays a benefit tied to school attendance and clinic visits and is supported by World Bank lending. The Inter-American Development Bank lends for education. Both were found on the lenders' project pages.

Recorded as findings

The latest national figure for households receiving remittances, 55.9%, dates from 2019, and the full report is sold rather than free.
